content:
PLEASE Think Twice Before Booking This Tour!
This Was One of the Worst Experiences of Our Lives. During the Sunset Tour, Our Boat Capsized in the Open Sea, and We Were Left Waiting in the Water for Around 45 Minutes Until Local Fishermen Finally Rescued Us.
We Lost Our Phones and All of Our Personal Belongings. Despite the Financial and Emotional Impact, We Felt That We Received No Meaningful Support. To Make Matters Worse, We Were Even Asked to Pay for the Tour After the Accident.
After the Incident, the Company Told Us That the Person Operating the Boat Was Not Their Regular Captain. Hearing This Raised Even More Concerns About Their Safety Standards.
Please Don’t Take Chances With Your Safety. Before Booking, Ask Who Will Be Operating the Boat and What Safety Measures Are in Place. Based on Our Experience, We Cannot Recommend This Company.

content:
I was here as part of a tour offered by my hotel. The sandbank itself is almost unrealistically beautiful and certainly deserves more than one star. Surrounding it are many corals and small reefs teeming with sea urchins and fish. And that's where the trouble really begins.
Every day, tourists are ferried in by boat for lunch and presumably dinner as well. Tables, chairs, and grills are set up (what an effort!) to offer seafood. The trash was collected, at least roughly.
What I found particularly disturbing was the way nature was treated. Tourists were touching corals, plastic bottles were lying everywhere, and there was constant noise. The boats were crashing into existing coral colonies, and animals were being actively caught to show the tourists.
Of course, there was no shade, except for the sails people brought with them. The temperature climbed to around 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit), and I'm surprised no one collapsed. The white sand and its reflection made the sun simply unbearable. Everyone on the tour got a terrible sunburn, despite using sunscreen.
Once all the boats had arrived (around 50), it looked like a scene from a beach resort. No one was drinking alcohol, though; I suspect people were afraid of passing out. Instead, it was loud and crowded, which didn't do justice to this unique landscape at all.
I thought it was awful and just longed for the trip to end.
Bad tourism.

content: A rip-off for tourists. $30 for foreigners (30,000 shillings for locals), although that's still a lot... You arrive at the park, pay at reception, wait 15-20 minutes for a guide to be available (not a group trip, but solo or with family), and off you go. The first stop is a cage with 4 turtles where you can touch them and take photos, the second stop is a pen with 2 antelopes + 2 young giraffes + 2 zebras. You can feed each one and take a photo. The third stop is a square with pigeons. They give you food in your hand and take photos with the pigeons sitting in your hands. That's it!) 20 minutes maximum. It's interesting if you want to feel like you're in a petting zoo for 20 minutes for $30 and get some nice photos. There's no care for the animals here. They're kept here specifically (brought from the mainland) to make money.

content:
I visited Zakir Wildlife in Zanzibar and unfortunately left very upset and concerned about the treatment of the animals.
There was a monkey there with a large, clearly visible wound on her tail. What concerned me even more was her reaction to the handler. She appeared very scared of him, while at the same time she was extremely gentle and friendly with us. She willingly came to us, lay down, and allowed us to cuddle and interact with her. The contrast between how comfortable she was with visitors and how frightened she appeared around the handler was very disturbing to witness.
We asked the staff directly why the monkey was injured and why she was not receiving treatment. We did not receive a clear or convincing answer.
Afterwards, we contacted Zakir Wildlife through Instagram because we were genuinely concerned about her welfare. They told us that the monkey was at the vet.
It has now been about a month, and this monkey is no longer there, but theres no clear information what happened to her or whether she actually received proper treatment.
I sincerely hope she is alive, safe, and receiving veterinary care. However, the lack of transparency and the original condition of the animal are extremely concerning.
I am leaving this review because wildlife tourism should be about protecting and caring for animals, not simply allowing tourists to interact with them. If an animal has a serious visible wound, visitors deserve a clear explanation that appropriate veterinary care is being provided.
I strongly encourage anyone considering visiting to ask questions about the animals’ welfare and veterinary care before supporting this place

content:
What an incredible experience! 💙
After how much fun we had the first time, we decided to repeat the excursion… and it was even better! We swam with the dolphins again, and our guide did everything possible to ensure we could enjoy them for as long as possible. He was so attentive and professional that one of my children even got to touch one of the dolphins. When he came out of the water, he said, laughing, “It was hard and slippery!” 🤣🤣 A moment we'll never forget.
Afterward, we went fishing, and when we finished, they took us to a local house where they cooked the fish we had just caught in the most traditional way. It was an authentic experience, very different from any restaurant, and undoubtedly one of the most special moments of the trip.
The food was delicious: octopus in sauce, breaded octopus with a local recipe whose exact ingredients we don't know, but it was spectacular!, salad, sweet plantain… Everything prepared with so much love. I'm sharing a photo because, as they say, a picture is worth a thousand words.
The family who hosted us was lovely. They didn't speak English, and we didn't speak their language, but that wasn't a problem at all. Sometimes you don't need to speak the same language to understand each other. Their hospitality, their smiles, and the warmth with which they treated us said it all.
Thank you from the bottom of our hearts for giving us memories that will stay with us for a lifetime. If you're thinking about taking a trip with them, don't hesitate. We went back... and we would do it again a thousand times!

content:
We booked a snorkeling tour to Mnemba Island on June 18, 2026. The tour was very well organized, and we were picked up from the beach right on time. Plenty of fruit and water were provided along the way.
Unfortunately, our guide's English wasn't very good, making communication rather difficult, and there weren't many explanations.
Another issue was that the tour took us to places that were absolutely overrun with other tour boats. The snorkeling spot was so crowded that we were afraid of colliding with another boat.
When we visited the sandbar, we were able to anchor a little away from the hustle and bustle, which was truly wonderful.
When the topic of a possible dolphin sighting came up, we were shocked. Two dolphins appeared and were practically chased by all the boats (around 20 of them). People were jumping into the water to swim with them. Thankfully, the two dolphins took flight. After that, we didn't feel like looking for any more. Visiting another beach further north was nice enough, but ultimately we didn't quite understand what we were supposed to be doing there. Since the guide's English wasn't good enough, he couldn't really explain it. All the boats went there, and behind the beach was a market selling nothing but tourist trinkets – definitely not worth the trip. It was completely overcrowded.
All in all, we wouldn't book this tour again. The lovely visit to the sandbank and the rather scenic boat trip along the coast unfortunately couldn't compensate for the other negative experiences.

We first met Abdillah during a tour to Stone Town and Prison Island and were so impressed by his service that we wanted to book a second tour with him. This time, we visited Jozani Forest.
Jozani Forest, the largest and only protected rainforest on the island, is truly fascinating. It’s home to the Red Colobus monkeys, which are native only to Zanzibar. The rainforest is impressive for its diverse flora and fauna, and although not originally native, the mahogany trees are a beautiful sight.
We were lucky enough to see a large group of Red Colobus monkeys up close. Unfortunately, we couldn’t visit the part of the jungle with the mangroves, as it was inaccessible due to the high tide.
All in all, it was another great day with Abdi. We felt well taken care of, and he treated us with water and great company.
Thank you, Abdi! You are such a kind person, and we would gladly book more tours with you and highly recommend you to others!

content: Old Slave Market - today, this site is home to a Catholic cathedral and a monument erected in honor of the victims of slavery. It is known that in the mid-19th century, approximately 40,000 slaves passed through Zanzibar annually. The British put an end to this practice in the late 19th century, and Bishop Edward Steere, whose body rests in the cathedral, took an active part in the fight against slavery. The descent into the cells where men, women, and children were held before the auction is shocking. A cell measuring 5x3 meters - without water, access to fresh air, or food - held 50 men or 75 women and children. Those who survived these inhumane conditions were put up for auction. Those who survived proved to be the "strongest" - "people dealt this fate to people," as always.

clauses.clause_text: Those who survived these inhumane conditions were put up for auction.

content:
The Anglican church, Christ Church Cathedral, was built on the site of a former slave market in Stone Town (in the old part of Zanzibar City, the capital of Zanzibar – the Stone Town area was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000). What shocked me most was the fact that the slave trade was abolished by order of the Sultan only at the end of the 19th century, in 1873!
Zanzibar was under Portuguese rule from the late 15th century until 1698, when the island was taken over by the Sultans of Oman. It then became a center of trade, including the slave trade – due to its strategically advantageous geographical location in the Indian Ocean, Europeans eagerly sourced labor for their colonies. According to historians' estimates, between 1830 and 1873, approximately 600,000 people were sold here as merchandise, and many more slaves were held here en route to their destinations. It was the largest slave market in East Africa.
In 1861, Zanzibar became a British colony. By then, many activists were campaigning for the abolition of slavery. British (Scottish) explorer and physician David Livingstone, as well as Anglican Bishop Edward Steere, were particularly active. After the final abolition of slavery in 1873, Bishop Steere laid the foundation stone for a church intended to symbolize freedom from tyranny. The cathedral, completed in 1879, is built of coral reef stones, combining various architectural styles with distinct local and Arabic accents.
Zanzibar seceded from the British Empire in 1963. In January 1964, a revolution took place, resulting in the country becoming the independent Republic of Zanzibar and Pemba. Three months later, in April of that year, it formed a new state – Tanzania – with the Republic of Tanganyika, while retaining significant autonomy (including a separate government and president).
Next to the cathedral stands the Slave Memorial, created by Swedish sculptor Clara Sörnäs in 1998. Since 2006, the East African Slave Market exhibition has been open – a visit forces one to reflect on humanity. Visitors can see, among other things, two rooms in the damp and cold basements where slaves were held in incredibly cramped conditions, as well as an exhibition of materials and photographs relating to this shameful practice (the transport of slaves, the trade, their destinations, the abolition of slavery, and the new forms of slavery occurring in the 21st century).

content:
To wade through the history of Zanzibar move a little north towards Bububu and reach Mtoni Palace Ruins. It islocated just north of Maruhubi, built between 1828 and 1834 for Sultan Said. The land believed to be belonged to Saleh bin Haramil, the Arab trader who imported the first cloves to Zanzibar. Mtoni means ‘place by the river’. This is the oldest Palace in Zanzibar.
Read the history before you are there.
One of Sultan Said’s daughters, Princess Salme later took the name Emily Ruete in her book, describes Mtoni Palace in the 1850s and her life.
Salama bint Said was born on 30 August 1844 and she spent her initial years in huge Mtoni Palace, 8km north of Stone Town. After parents death she moved to Kisimbani, one of her estates. Finally moving to Stone Town. Here she became close to her neighbor, a German merchant, Rudolph Heinrich Ruete (born 10 March 1839; died 6 August 1870) and became pregnant by him. She fled to Germany. Her memoirs give insight into the history of Zanzibar.
Feel the history of beautiful Zanzibar with reading it and visiting the place. Good luck.

content:
I had a great experience with Coconuts Kite in Zanzibar. I took 12 hours of lessons with Mageni, and I couldn’t have asked for a better instructor. He was incredibly patient and made sure I felt safe at all times, carefully explaining all the security aspects of kitesurfing. His calm and reassuring attitude really helped me gain confidence in the water.
Elisa was also fantastic — always easy to reach and very responsive. We communicated daily on WhatsApp to organize the lesson times according to my availability and the tide conditions, which made everything smooth and stress-free.
Depending on the tide, I was able to practice either directly from the beach or in the lagoon, which was a great advantage as a beginner. The entire staff was super friendly and welcoming, creating a relaxed and supportive atmosphere.
The equipment is not the newest, but as a beginner, it was absolutely sufficient and perfectly suitable for learning.
I highly recommend Coconuts Kite to anyone looking to learn or improve their kitesurfing skills in Zanzibar!

The training is thought out down to the last detail, very professional, and safe. Elise, the school's director, is very attentive and incredibly kind. content:
If disappointment were a water sport, Coconuts Kite Zanzibar would be world champions.
From the moment I arrived, it felt less like a kite school and more like an experiment in how little effort can be stretched over an entire day. Organization was apparently optional, communication was a fun guessing game, and time moved at its own mysterious pace—mostly backward.
The vibe? Imagine enthusiasm being actively discouraged. Any questions were met with the kind of silence usually reserved for awkward elevators. Equipment looked like it had lived several previous lives and was now just tired of existing.
The beach itself is beautiful—though that’s entirely Zanzibar’s fault and in no way thanks to Coconuts. In fact, the highlight of the experience was realizing that simply standing still and staring at the ocean was infinitely more rewarding than engaging with anything offered here.
If you enjoy confusion, waiting around for no clear reason, and wondering how a place managed to get such a good location while doing absolutely nothing with it, then congratulations—you’ve found your spot.
Everyone else: do yourself a favor and keep walking. The wind deserves better.

content:
Our experience in Jambiani was unfortunately overshadowed by constant harassment from some beach vendors. Saying “no” was often not respected. We were repeatedly approached, whistled at to get our attention, and sometimes followed or pressured to continue the conversation after refusing. Instead of feeling able to relax, we felt we had to stay on guard whenever we walked along the beach.
We were also uncomfortable seeing children approach tourists asking for money or trying to attract attention. Whether encouraged by adults or not, it created an uneasy atmosphere and raised concerns about the involvement of children in tourist interactions.
We found that several beachfront restaurants offered disappointing value for money, with prices that felt high compared with the portion sizes served. In contrast, local restaurants away from the beachfront, e.g. Banana restaurant, provided better meals and better value during our stay. We also found that the Blue Oyster - beachfront - is really receptive to feedback and the food is delicious
The beach itself is beautiful, and many local residents going about their daily work, such as fishermen and seaweed harvesters, were respectful and did not disturb visitors. However, travellers looking for a peaceful and uninterrupted beach experience should be aware that this was not our experience in parts of Jambiani, and because of the above we don’t recommend Zanzibar.

Zanzibar/Jambiani has real beauty — I’ve visited three times in five years because I wanted to believe in it. I won’t be returning.
The beach experience has deteriorated significantly. Declining vendors is now met with hostility, passive-aggressive comments, and verbal abuse. Not occasionally — consistently. “La asante” and walking away no longer works.
The food situation is equally frustrating. Restaurants are charging European prices for portions that wouldn’t satisfy a child. You’re paying Lisbon prices for a quarter of the plate.
If you’re coming to genuinely rest and recover, manage your expectations carefully. The paradise you see in photos requires a lot of work to access — and increasingly, it’s not worth the effort.

content: This wide beach is perfect for a quiet, intimate getaway away from the larger resorts and large tourist groups. Located in the southeastern part of the island, it's far from the major resorts. Even in peak season, it's relatively quiet, and everyone can find a secluded spot away from other beachgoers. There are fewer Maasai than in other locations. Jambiani stretches for over 2 km. It's entirely covered in fine, snow-white sand that resembles powder. The ocean water is crystal clear and warm, but the bottom isn't exclusively sandy; both small stones and larger boulders can appear. Starfish, crabs, and sea urchins are often found on the shore. Therefore, wearing special rubber water shoes is recommended. The beach is also often covered with algae, brought in by the strong tides that occur in this area. Furthermore, it's worth knowing that the tides here are quite high. During this time, only sunbathing is possible, not swimming in the ocean. If you love beautiful beaches, exciting attractions, good restaurants with delicious food and authenticity, you will love this place.

content:
We departed from Nungwi by tuk-tuk for 20,000 shillings roundtrip and reached the cave in 20 minutes. The driver was waiting for us.
Here, you can not only visit two large caves but also a small chameleon farm. Zanzibar Island was once underwater, a seabed; millions of years ago, shifting plate formations pushed the island up, and these caves are clear evidence of this area's marine past. Millions of years ago, seawater currents created these labyrinths. Once on the surface, and gradually covered with a layer of organic matter, these caves became filled with land dwellers—bats and insects. According to the guide, traces of ancient human habitation were also found here, namely clay cooking utensils. Gradually, groundwater flowed into the crevices of the rocks, forming stalactites under the cave roofs, some of which are over 1,000 years old. Water is still gently dripping, so you can see the process of creating these bizarre shapes. I should note that I wouldn't recommend the second cave for older people or children. Since it's not a walk-through cave, there's a feeling of air shortage, a steep descent, and many of the passages are very narrow or low. The second cave is definitely not suitable for those with a fear of confined spaces. The first cave is quite comfortable to visit. A guide accompanies you throughout the tour and explains everything in great detail and interest. Flashlights are also provided. The video shows how the flashlights illuminate beautiful sections of the cave walls and ceiling, allowing you to admire the lacework of white crystals that completely cover the walls and ceiling. You can discern the outlines of various virtual animals, such as a turtle, a snail, a shark, or a giant baobab tree. A visit to the cave costs $10, but add another $5 for a visit to a wonderful small chameleon farm. The total time is at least an hour.

content: In Nungwi, where the northernmost shores of Zanzibar meet the vast Indian Ocean, the beach hums with a rhythm that feels eternal. The sands, cool and fine underfoot, stretch endlessly, kissed by water so clear it mirrors the sky. Fishermen anchor their dhows after the day’s work, their wooden boats carrying whispers of centuries-old traditions. Nearby, a local artisan threads beads onto bracelets, her fingers moving deftly as laughter ripples from children chasing the tide. The air is warm, scented faintly of salt and the smoke of seafood grills along the shore. By twilight, the world seems to pause—only the sound of waves and murmured conversations remain. Nungwi is not merely a beach; it is an experience of connection: to the land, to its people, and to the stories carried in every grain of sand.

content:
The Old Fort in Stone Town is one of those places where history is literally beneath your feet.
Thick coral stone walls, darkened by time, the scent of the sea, old limestone, and something spicy—all of this instantly transports you back to the era when Zanzibar was a center of the spice and slave trade.
The fort was built in the late 17th century by Arabs from the Sultanate of Oman. They had just recaptured the island from the Portuguese and were strengthening their position. They maintained a garrison here, defended the harbor, then served as a prison, and later even as a warehouse and train station when the British arrived with their own rules.
This place has a rich history, full of changes, like Zanzibar itself.
Today, the fort looks stern, but vibrant.
Inside is an amphitheater where concerts and festivals are held, surrounded by souvenir and spice stalls, women selling fabrics, and children kicking a ball around.
You sit on a rock, looking at the towers, listening to someone singing in Swahili, and you realize that history hasn't stopped here—it's just shifted to a different rhythm.
I climbed the wall and looked down at the old town—white facades, tin roofs, the sea in the distance. And I thought: Zanzibar isn't just an island, it's a place where everything has mixed—Arabs, Africans, Indians, Europeans—and each has left their mark. The old fort stands as a reminder of this—rough, beautiful, and honest.

content: Built around 1700 by SeyyidSeif bin Sultan of Ya’aruba Dynasty who ruled Oman from 1692 to 1711 D. This site was once occupied by Portuguese chapel and small fortified houses before their total expulsion from East Africa in 1698. The Oman Arabs replaced the Portuguese remnants by construction of western side of the fort. Some of chapel remnants can be seen on north western corner wall of the fort until today. In 1836, Seyyid Said himself added eastern half of the fort for the purpose of keeping his garrison. The Omanis partially demolished the Portuguese chapel and a Portuguese merchant house and incorporated them in the construction of what was described in 1710 as a ridiculous little Fort. In the later years it was used as a prison. In 1905, the fort was used as a railway station and a deport. The front passage was constructed in 1946 to house ladies club. From 1964, it is used for cultural performances. Currently, it is a home for several festivals such as ZIFF, Sauti za Busara (Sound of Wisdom) etc.

Stone Town - Zanzibar, visited on November 12, 2022. The fort was built by the Arabs in the 17th century. In the 19th century, it served as a prison, then a railway station for the legendary Bububu railway, and later a tennis court for wealthy English tourists.
Now you can visit the courtyard, where many vendors offer their wares to tourists. The interior is closed to the public. Unfortunately, little is being done to preserve the building. The House of Miracles is located nearby.

content:
Our visit to Freddie Mercury Museum was a special and slightly nostalgic experience, especially if you’re a fan of music or someone who appreciates cultural history.
Located right in the heart of Stone Town, the museum sits in the very house where Freddie Mercury (born Farrokh Bulsara) spent his early years before moving abroad. That itself makes the visit quite meaningful — you’re literally stepping into a place connected to one of the greatest musical legends of all time.
The museum is relatively small, but thoughtfully curated. It showcases photographs, personal stories, handwritten lyrics, and memorabilia that trace Freddie Mercury’s journey — from his childhood in Zanzibar and schooling in India to his rise as the iconic frontman of Queen. ￼
It doesn’t take very long to explore (roughly 20–40 minutes), but if you take your time reading through everything, it becomes a much richer experience.
Opening hours: 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM daily ￼
Duration: Less than an hour is usually enough ￼
Entry fee: $10 for non-residents (approx.) ￼
One thing to keep in mind — this is not a large or highly interactive museum. It’s more of a compact, personal tribute rather than an expansive exhibition. So managing expectations helps.
We found it to be a nice stop while exploring Stone Town — especially given its central location, making it easy to combine with nearby attractions. The experience is more about appreciating the roots and early life of Freddie Mercury rather than expecting a grand museum setup.
Overall, if you’re even remotely a fan of Queen or enjoy music history, it’s definitely worth a short visit. It adds a unique cultural layer to your Zanzibar experience.

clauses.clause_text: Duration: Less than an hour is usually enough ￼
Entry fee: $10 for non-residents (approx.) ￼

content:
You stand in this house, close your eyes, and suddenly everything is there.
Not as an exhibition.
Not as an object.
But as movement within.
The walls disappear, time loses its sharpness, and somewhere between the first note and the second heartbeat, something begins that is greater than memory. A voice rises, not loudly, but necessarily. It no longer bears a name; it carries people. Millions. It lifts them up, makes them stomp, laugh, cry, recognize each other. We will rock you—not as a title, but as a promise. A rhythm that rises through your legs, through your chest, until you realize that you've been participating all along, without being asked.
Here, in these narrow rooms, nothing matters except one thing:
A person has decided not to let their life be small.
Farrokh becomes Freddie.
Not by chance, but through courage.
Through getting up every day against fear, against doubt, against loneliness.
Through the will to make one's origins not a prison, but a springboard.
Through the quiet decision to trust one's own voice until it grows strong enough to carry others.
You see photographs, letters, sheet music—and suddenly you understand:
It's not about originals.
It's about truth.
The music didn't move the world because it was perfect,
but because it was honest.
Because it came from within, willing to risk everything to be real.
And in that moment, when you stand still and listen to the songs resonate within your own body, you realize:
The miracle was never the museum.
The miracle was humanity.
A single spark that was enough to set millions in motion.
Not through volume.
But through authenticity.
And something within us recognizes itself in this.
Not as a fan.
Not as a tourist.
But as a person who senses:
My life, too, is bigger than I've allowed myself to believe.
You leave not with a souvenir,
but with a decision in your heart:
To no longer keep your own life small.
And that's precisely why it works.
Because you don't want to react—
but have to.

content:
The Freddie Mercury Museum: A Bittersweet Disappointment
As a Freddie Mercury fan, my visit to the museum left me with mixed feelings, leaning towards disappointment. While it's exciting to have a space dedicated to a legend like him, the experience is marred by two major problems.
The first, and most hurtful, is the hypocrisy of a museum celebrating the life of a gay icon like Freddie existing and profiting in a country where homosexuality is prohibited and criminalized. It's an unacceptable contradiction that borders on exploitation, and as a fan and a gay man, it fills me with deep indignation. How is it possible that they profit from his legacy while people are persecuted and oppressed for being who they are in this country? This situation completely overshadows any positive aspects of the visit.
Furthermore, the museum is expensive for what it offers. The collection is quite limited and doesn't justify the entrance fee. Perhaps I was expecting something more profound about Freddie's life and work, but what you find is a modest exhibition that leaves you wanting more. The value for money is poor, which only intensifies the feeling that they're exploiting Freddie's name without offering anything worthy of him.
In short, for me it was a bittersweet and somewhat frustrating experience. The moral dilemma and the high price mean I can't enthusiastically recommend it to other fans. I'm sorry.

content: Finally, a museum dedicated to Freddie Mercury in his homeland. Little is known about Freddie's early years, as he was born in Stone Town's public hospital on September 5, 1946. Almost nothing is known about his childhood in Zanzibar and India, and even less about the Zoroastrian religion followed by the Parsi community to which his family belonged. In this museum, you can find answers to many of your questions, discover many unpublished photos, and insights into Zanzibar society at the time, the Zoroastrian religion, and the Parsi community. There's also, of course, tons of memorabilia, drawings by Freddie, lyrics from songs he wrote himself, stage costumes, and much more! If you go to Zanzibar, you absolutely must stop by.

Zanzibar tourist operators take the cake when it comes to charging loads for little to nothing. Soon, people will stop coming - there doesnt seem to be much understanding that an experience has to be provided, and tourists are not just cash cows. Better off paying for a cocktail at the hotel bar, you'll enjoy it more...

content: Our experience in Zanzibar has culminated with a visit to Zanzibar’s only national park. The tourist experience is generally, terribly organised, unless you are the social media generation, which will be happy taking mobile phone images of the tame monkeys near the reception. They then get back into the minibuses and leave. The guides and authorities are colluding with this ignorance and are becoming de-skilled. We had to persuade and persist getting a guide to escort us into the forest. Our visit was redeemed with an excellent guide called Adam. He was buoyed by our motivation and enthusiasm. We feel that the best way to enjoy the forest is to get there well before the throngs of tourists and do the half day hike.

content: A hopeless place, totally not worth the money. Let's start by saying that before I arrived, I asked a friend from Zanzibar who knows the island and its attractions very well about this place, and he replied that if I went anywhere else and took a path into the forest, of which there's no shortage, it would be exactly the same as this park. We pay $12 for the entrance fee and another $10 for a guided tour. The guide leads us through the bushes for 40 minutes, telling us stories about the surrounding plants, trees, and remnants of the reef. Unfortunately, this place truly deserves the name "bushes." I managed to see five monkeys, and of course, I understand that they don't wait for tourists and that it's accidental, but I would have seen the same monkeys if I had stood patiently by the main road. Part of the route to the mangrove forest lies outside the park. There are local homes there, and the monkeys sit in their yards like dogs. This road is directly opposite the park entrance. At the end, the guide mentions several times that you can tip him generously for what I consider a rather dubious walk through the thicket. I suggest spending that money on something better. Like food.

content:
We decided to take a half-day trip that included a stop at Jozani Chwaka Bay National Park. The journey itself was already quite an experience, offering a firsthand glimpse into the reality of corruption, with around 8–10 police checkpoints seemingly set up just to collect bribes. While this is worth mentioning, it does not influence our rating of the park itself.
The park is undeniably beautiful, showcasing lush nature and a rich variety of flora and fauna. It was a pleasure to observe the animals in their natural habitat, and our guide provided plenty of interesting information about the different plant species.
Unfortunately, the negative aspects outweighed the positives for us:
Mass tourism: Visitors are herded through the park in groups of approximately 40 people, which significantly diminishes the experience.
Tipping culture: Even during the initial briefing, there was already a strong emphasis on tipping the guide.
Disregard for rules: While sensible rules are explained—such as keeping a respectful distance from the monkeys—they are largely ignored. Most visitors end up crowding the animals, and the guides do little to enforce these guidelines.
Littering: One of the rules is to avoid leaving trash behind, which is ironic considering the park is littered with plastic waste. Rangers don’t seem to take any initiative to clean up or maintain the area.
In the end, Jozani Chwaka Bay National Park felt like just another location in Zanzibar being exploited to the maximum for tourism. A real shame, considering the natural beauty and ecological importance of the area.

Jozani Park or Jozani Forest is the largest National Park on the island of Unguja (Zanzibar). Here you can observe several species of monkeys, including the rare Red Colobus - an endemic species that is found only on the island of Unguja. They are characterized by the fact that they do not eat ripe fruit and have only four fingers. Along with the monkeys, you can also meet a miniature frog (adults are up to about a centimeter long), an elephant shrew, over 200 species of butterflies, land crabs, biting ants and many other interesting animals. You will also get to know many plants, huge trees laden with mangoes (the fruit's bark is a favorite of the Red Colobus), eucalyptus, tamarind, etc.
Be sure to visit the mangrove forest.
A wonderful place for walking, taking pictures and getting to know different types of plants and animals.

I didn't particularly enjoy this visit. It might be interesting for someone who has never seen monkeys before, but otherwise, I don't think the ticket price is worth it. I did the short tour, which lasts about 75 minutes, so I can't comment on the longer treks.
What bothered me most was that tourists were allowed to get far too close to the colobus monkeys. Some even went so far as to press themselves against them to take selfies. This is undoubtedly stressful for the monkeys and clearly disrupts their behavior.
The monkeys stay close to groups of tourists, hoping to get food, which is also undesirable.
The mangrove section is a bit more interesting, and at least the animals are left undisturbed there.
However, the road leading to the mangrove is in very poor condition. It's a shame, because with the revenue generated by the park, we could at least maintain it a little better.

The tour then begins with a short walk through the forest, during which our guide seemed to be rushing. However, we did manage to see our first monkeys.

All the explanations seemed rehearsed and simply recited.
At the end, the promised tip was collected.
All in all, the tour lasted about an hour.

content:
Experiences from the 3-hour tour:
Jungle:
Beautiful jungle with countless mahogany trees (I'd never seen anything like them before). Lots of monkeys, tiny frogs (they're amazingly small and very cute!), butterflies, and birds. We only noticed the snakes by their rustling. This was perfectly fine with the venomous green mambas and Indian cobras, and the (non-venomous) 6-meter pythons.
The mangroves at the end of the tour were very impressive, but require an additional 15-minute walk each way in the sun.
Clothing: I would recommend closed shoes (absolutely essential) and, despite the heat, long clothing (personal opinion), as we were actually a bit afraid of the venomous snakes – probably unfounded, since the snakes slither away before people get too close.
It was very hot (late September) and we had to do a lot of walking in the tropical heat, sometimes on dusty roads with no shade.
In conclusion: three hours was a bit long for the experience, but I wouldn't have wanted to miss the mangrove forests. I don't know if the mangroves are included in the one-hour tour.

content:
Extremely disappointed, we live in Zanzibar and we do not recommend this place. The forest is supposed to be visited with a guide, but most guides just take you around a roadside area to see three millipedes and two monkeys. It's a tourist trap like few others. Josiani is supposed to have a mangrove, a large forest, etc.
Before paying at the entrance, we were told that it was possible to visit without a guide (the regulations are posted after the entrance where you pay, so it's impossible to see them). Then, once we paid, we were told it was impossible without a guide (which we completely understood). We then asked for our money back so we could leave without visiting, since we were at the entrance and hadn't seen anything yet. And then, because it's easier to take money but more complicated to give it back, what followed was a series of incoherent and false explanations designed to lead us in circles and make us give up. Then, seeing that we were standing firm and remaining very calm, the staff and a guide began to threaten and verbally abuse us in a racist manner: "You'll never get your money back, leave, this isn't Europe, this is Africa," they laughed. Imagine if we had said the same thing to a Tanzanian visitor? "This isn't Africa, this is Europe, so leave!"... I absolutely do not recommend this place. There are many other places on the island, less than 5 km away, where you can see monkeys and a couple of woodlice with a much more respectful attitude. Avoid at all costs.

content: We were really disappointed with this place. I don't recommend going there. The entrance fee is 25,000 Tanzanian shillings, not including the mandatory, limited tip for the guide. When you reach the junction where you're supposed to turn left into the forest, I advise you to take the road on the right, because that's where the monkeys are. This way you'll avoid paying the 25,000 entrance fee unnecessarily. You can't get lost; it's a straight road. You'll see the monkeys on your right near the huts of the local people. A little further on, you'll find the mangrove where you can take a short 5-minute walk. That's the gist of it. The guide's three-sentence summary is practically useless. So unless you're a mahogany enthusiast, I advise against visiting Jozani Forest. It's much better to explore the monkeys and mangroves on your own...

The leaves and trunks have thorns, and the branches are barbed. You should dress accordingly; flip-flops won't get you far. Long pants are also a good idea if you don't want scratched feet. Definitely bring water! Along the way, the guide told us a lot about the plants and animals in the national park. One section of the path was swarming with ants, and our guide simply said, "You have to RUN!" It actually worked quite well. The smaller mangrove forest is also beautiful.

content:
English text below
Jozani is one of the few places in Zanzibar where nature is taken care of and protected in the sense we understand it in Europe. So you can only move around here with a guide and you definitely won't pick or pet anything here (which is only good). The park is divided into three parts, between which you need to drive a short distance by car. In the first you will find a rainforest with many plants. Some of them you may know from Europe, but more like small plants and not big trees like here. The second part is probably the most popular. Here are monkeys that you can observe very closely. Be careful, you are not allowed to feed or touch them. But it is still an experience. And the last part is the mangrove forest. Here it depends a lot on whether the tide is high or low. We were lucky with low tide, so you could see a tangle of roots and many crabs among them.
We can recommend a visit, it is a very nice place with nice people.
English
Jozani is one of the few places in Zanzibar where nature and its conservation are taken into consideration in the sense that we understand in Europe. So, you can only move around here with a guide, and you definitely won't be allowed to pick or touch anything (which is a good thing). The park is divided into three parts, between which you need to drive a short distance by car. In the first part, you'll find a jungle with many plants. Some of them you might recognize from Europe, but they're more like small plants rather than big trees, as they are here. The second part is probably the most popular. Here, you can observe monkeys very closely. Beware, you're not allowed to feed them or touch them. But even so, it's quite an experience. The last part is the mangrove forest. It greatly depends on whether it's high tide or low tide. We were lucky to have low tide, so we could see the tangle of roots and many crabs among them.
We can recommend the visit; it's a very beautiful place with friendly people.

However, we quickly abandoned that idea, because as soon as we parked our scooter, a guide approached us and explained that only guided tours were available. Naturally, this guide wanted us to join his tour. The tour lasted about an hour and consisted of three parts. First, a short walk through the national park, then we crossed the road to see the red clobus monkeys, which were already being admired by other tourists. Afterward, the taxis for the other tour participants were called, and we were driven to the mangroves. There's a circular walking trail there. After we completed the trail, the guide asked for a tip. We got the impression that our guide was reciting a memorized script at a very rapid pace. Later, we walked back to the scooter and revisited the spot with the monkeys. This time we didn't see any monkeys, but also no other tourists.

content:
We booked a tour through the hotel.
We took the short tour (with several people who met at reception).
Our guide, Amour, went to great lengths to tell us a lot about the forest, its influences, and the surrounding area.
Typical of the tourist world, the tour focuses heavily on showcasing the forest's classic feature—the monkeys. Finding them was the goal of the tour.
The tour lasted just over an hour, through the forest and mangroves.
I think the quality of the tour depends a lot on the guide. We were very lucky and will definitely do a longer tour with our guide—a deeper dive into nature with more forest inhabitants.
A little tip: Many in our group didn't quite manage it. Flip-flops aren't suitable footwear for a jungle. And if a guide tells you to keep your distance from the animals, you should heed their advice.

content:
Interesting and definitely recommended. My tip, addressing the previous reviews: Don't book through the tour operators at the hotel. Book a private guide. This way, you can decide how long you want to spend at each stop. It worked perfectly for us over two days, and I can't understand the €150 per person mentioned here. For €100, we saw Changuu Island, Stone Town (including the museum), the Spice Farms, the Zaaso Animal Welfare Organization, Jozani Forest, and the Nungwi Aquarium over two full days (it's impossible to do it all in one day). This included entrance fees, a private guide, a private driver, and drinks. Highly recommended. I'm happy to help if you're interested.
Now, about Jozani Forest. If you take your time there, you have the opportunity to observe the monkeys up close. It's really recommended for photographers. The mangrove forest on the other side, with its natural boardwalk, is also beautifully laid out and worth a visit.

content: We visited Jozani Forest Park in Zanzibar in August 2018. There you can see blue and red koula monkeys. The blue ones live solitary lives, while the red ones live in groups. We visited the small park with our guide in the morning and saw many monkeys. With a bit of luck, the red koula monkeys are all gathered in one spot, and you can observe them up close as they climb, hang from branches, or enjoy eating leaves. You are not allowed to touch or feed them. They won't hurt you and seem to enjoy being photographed, remaining completely undisturbed. There were also some baby monkeys when we were there. There's a forest you walk through where you might spot a blue koula or two. We highly recommend a visit to this park. The entrance fee is $5 per person. It's an amazing experience to be so close to a monkey.

content:
We booked this excursion as a hotel tour with air-conditioned bus service from the Royal Zanz Beach Resort.
The bus wasn't full, which was very pleasant. We had a total of three guides through Fisherman Tours (an experienced local operator), who spoke English, German, and Swahili.
The drive to Jozani and Prison Island was very interesting; you can see the local life firsthand along the road. From the construction of huts and houses to the dalla-dalla buses of the locals and the tuk-tuks carrying countless workers and market vendors... the tour guides are very knowledgeable and answer all our questions.
In the Jozani and mangrove area, it looked like another planet to us. (It looks as if the earth acts as a saltwater filter, allowing life to develop there over the centuries.) It was a short but interesting excursion. The short hike along the boardwalks was quite interesting and varied. We continued walking through the forest for a while afterward.
The past was briefly explained here as well.
All in all, in short: a great day trip for $70-90 per person. A welcome change from the usual hotel routine.
Highlights:
- Bus ride
- Very close encounter with red colobus monkeys
- Hike along the boardwalks
- Hike through the jungle
Best regards and have a nice day

content: As a nature lover, I loved the forests and the monkeys. The guides were quite knowledgeable and I heard them explaining details of the forest in a number of different languages. I liked the idea that a percentage of the proceeds from the park fees go to help the local community. Why shouldn't the locals benefit from tourism? As a resident of Tanzania, I see all too often the tourist dollars being funneled outside of the country with a minimal amount of benefit reaching the local residents. The park fee subsidizes local farmers and damage to their crops caused by allowing the monkeys to stay in their locality. Please be advised that there are signs posted on the highway prohibiting photographing the monkeys without paying the park fee. Do not risk losing your camera. This is a government law. Some might feel offended by this... feeling that their freedom is being restricted. They usually just want something for nothing. Be happy as you share in the conservation efforts of Jozani Forest.

We gave Juani Forest a miss after mixed reviews and opted for this instead.

A brief but a detailed discussion about the life cycle of butterflies and how they're farmed here, with lots of items to look at including the most incredible shiny golden chrysalis! You can then wander around the netted garden for as long as you want admiring the plants and butterflies and any other creatures you may find!
There's also another section outside the butterfly garden where they move the chameleons to (so they don't eat the butterflies) and we were able to hold a chameleon and watch them change colour.
100% worth a visit!

content:
Ich war in diesem Jahr zum 17. Mal auf dieser Insel und bin immer noch begeistert und neugierig, was das Riff mir Neues zu bieten hat. In diesem Jahr gelang es mir einen Papageienfisch zu dokumentieren, der bisher noch nicht in diesem Riff gefunden und identifiziert werden konnte. Für mich war das ein besonderer Moment!

Chumbe, die Insel und das Riff, ist ein besonderer Platz. Und wenn dieses Ideal sich nicht so zeigt, sind natürlich 'Andere'" schuld.

I was extremely disappointed by the treatment and behavior of the park staff. Based on my experience, I would not recommend visiting this place.
Before making the trip, I called the park and spoke with a staff member in English to ask about the ticket price. I was told it was 5,000 TSH. I repeated the question to make sure I had understood correctly, and they confirmed the same price.

We read good reviews and decided to visit this park with the kids. We arrived at 10:00 a.m. Our first disappointment awaited us at the entrance: the 5,000 entrance fee is only for Tanzanian residents. Although the website doesn't mention this at all. content:
My wife and I had such high expectations of this ‘trip’ but unfortunately the staff and organization seem to be the biggest downfall for our experience. When booking my wife did email to let the staff know that we would want picture opportunities together because let’s be honest the main attraction to this place is the photo/video opportunities, my wife even mentioned that we would be happy to pay extra for this. We were told there would be staff to help with this and it would be at no extra cost.
At no point do they inform you that there are NO opportunities to eat throughout the day, you are offered water and prosecco but no food, we were collected from our hotel at 12pm & didn’t arrive back to the hotel until 8:30pm, ideally if they had told us this when booking we could have arranged some form of pack lunch! My wife has health issues which means she has to eat throughout the day little and often, however when we told staff this they still made sure we put our bags into a reception office and just said ‘no sorry we don’t have food here, there isn’t anywhere you can get any food either’
Our group had a total of 21 guests which is way too many, this was discussed throughout the day with other guests and everyone said the same thing, the day is far longer than it needs to be because of the amount of people to animal ratio - 2 bush babies to 21 guests and everyone gets to feed them twice? Then 4 lemurs to 21 guests.. you can imagine the waiting around, we are avid animal lovers and have our own animal rescue rehab farm in the UK so we totally understand the day is controlled inevitably by the animals and how they are feeling but the animals weren’t the problem.
Staff who lead the tour were quite demeaning and rude, not to us as such but others it was quite embarrassing hearing how one man spoke to people. The staff who are in the black shirts (locals) were so pleasant and as helpful as can be.
When it came to the ‘main event’ the images with the beautiful Latifah OBVIOUSLY with myself and my wife being together and it also being our honeymoon we wanted our pictures to be together, with this being such an expensive trip too we wanted to be sure our only images were perfect. After our pictures were taken with the cheetah we then checked them and noticed every picture that was taken was blurry and their finger was infront of the camera, when we mentioned this to staff and asked if there was any chance we could try and just get one more we were told ‘No’
We were then split up for the next encounter so again my wife was allowed another picture but not with myself? I was able to brush the cheetah but not with my wife? It was all very badly organized and honestly not worth the money at all, many other people were told they couldn’t join in due to colours they were wearing? At no point was this sent or mentioned in the email so this other couple didn’t get to have any Involvement in some things which was such a shame. we felt like we had wasted a day of our holiday from start to finish with this trip. We have done experiences like this all over the world and we haven’t ever had this experience.
Honestly I wouldn’t recommend this trip to anyone, if it was ran by the local men it would have been such a nicer experience and this isn’t due to ‘rules’ at all we completely understand how it works. Just lack of communication and breakdown of the day prior to booking. If it was explained how it ACTUALLY would be, we would have saved our money and not bothered.
However one positive I can add is that the animals are all well taken care of and it is clear how clean enclosures are kept.

content:
We cannot recommend Cheetah's Rock highly enough!
My sister and I initially booked the Great Wildlife Tour, and we were so impressed that we immediately decided to book the VIP Otter Tour as well. Without a doubt, these were some of the most incredible experiences we have ever had.
One of the things that stood out the most was how much we learned about the animals. Having grown up with many animals ourselves, we are familiar with animal behaviour and care, but Jenny and her team still taught us an incredible amount. Their depth of knowledge and genuine passion for educating visitors, while sharing the unique stories of each animal, made the experience truly special.
The VIP Otter Tour is a private experience where, if the otters choose to interact, you even have the opportunity to play with them. During the Great Wildlife Tour, we met many different species, observed them up close, and, in some cases, interacted with them. At no point did it feel like the animals were being forced to perform for tourists.
What impressed us the most was that the welfare of every single animal always comes first. It is obvious that Jenny and her team are deeply passionate about what they do. The tours help fund the sanctuary and provide care for rescued animals, but every interaction is carefully considered and only takes place when it also benefits the animals.
For example, playing with the otters provides them with important enrichment and stimulation. Other interactions help animals become more comfortable with handling by veterinarians or caretakers, reducing stress when medical treatment is needed. Every animal is treated as an individual, and the team carefully considers whether an animal actually wants to interact with visitors. If an animal prefers not to participate, it is simply left alone. The animals always have the choice to walk away.
It is also clear how much trust exists between Jenny, her team, and the animals. You can immediately see that the animals have had positive experiences with their caretakers. Even during demonstrations, such as with the zebra, it was obvious that everything was based on trust rather than force, and the animals could leave the interaction whenever they wanted.
Beyond the tours themselves, the work this sanctuary does is truly inspiring. Many of the animals have been rescued from heartbreaking situations, saved from death, or given a second chance after suffering terrible circumstances. By booking a tour, you are directly supporting this important conservation and rescue work.
The only small criticism we have is not directed at Cheetah’s Rock, but at some of its visitors. Unfortunately, not everyone treats the animals with the care and respect they deserve. The team sometimes has to step in, and in our opinion, anyone who continues to behave disrespectfully should simply be asked to leave. We honestly cannot understand such disrespect towards these amazing animals and work of the team.
All in all: This was truly a once-in-a-lifetime experience, and we are so grateful we had the opportunity to visit. If you are traveling to Zanzibar or Tanzania, we wholeheartedly recommend booking one of these tours. And if you cannot visit, consider supporting this amazing sanctuary with a donation. Jenny and her team are doing extraordinary work, and they deserve every bit of support they can get.
Lara & Alicia

content:
Regarding the criticism in the previous review!
This criticism does not reflect the impression one gets on-site. The animal shelter is run with great dedication, and it is understandable that a significant portion of the income goes directly into the animals' care – for example, food, grooming, and medical treatment.
Another important aspect is the financing: The transport of the rescued animals is organized and paid for privately, as are all operating costs. There is apparently no government support. Veterinary services, supplies, and necessary medications are expensive, especially when certain items have to be flown in. Against this backdrop, the income appears to be a necessary foundation for the shelter's operation.
Furthermore, this is an institution that saves animals from being euthanized, as they are often no longer fit to be released into the wild. The responsibility encompasses not only the animals themselves but also the entire organizational and financial risk. All costs are covered independently, including the salaries of the staff, who provide daily care for the animals under professional supervision.
The living conditions also differ from the description in the review. The enclosures appear well-maintained and designed to meet the animals' needs. The absence of blankets in the cages reflects natural living conditions – animals in the wild also lie on soil, grass, or similar surfaces. The design aims to create an environment that is as natural as possible while also ensuring safety.
The facility serves to protect animals that are often no longer able to survive in the wild. The focus is on their care, stabilization, and – where possible – eventual release back into the wild.
The offered visits can also be seen as a contribution to funding and raising awareness about animal welfare. Overall, a much more nuanced picture emerges than presented in the initial criticism.
Finally, it is regrettable that platforms like Google are used for such reviews without any firsthand experience on-site or a demonstrable understanding of animal care. Reviews should ideally be honest, objective, and respectful. This standard is not met in the present criticism.
These reviews are also intended to be informative and supportive. After nine visits to Cheetahs Rock
It was one of the most impressive experiences I've ever had the privilege of witnessing. The way the animals are cared for there is truly remarkable. Everyone on the team has made it their mission to ensure these rare and beautiful creatures have everything they need. If more people did this, the world would be a better place. Every bit of support is invaluable.

content:
Sad but true. Our experience at Cheetha's Rock.
The responses to reviews/criticisms from owner Jenny sometimes read like the reactions of an unusually quick-tempered operator, rather than an objective assessment of visitor feedback.
The fact that criticism is quickly portrayed as a request for "special treatment" suggests a lack of openness to honest feedback.
The claim that interactions are based on the animals' natural rhythms also raises questions, especially when the animals are simultaneously presented in a highly staged manner.
The discrepancy between the stated goal and the reality is striking, at least to outsiders. In my opinion, the tone with customers is more patronizing than reflective, which gives the impression of a certain resistance to criticism on the part of the owner. On-site, I was reprimanded and embarrassed in front of a group of tourists, almost rudely and extremely unprofessionally, after I politely asked if I could take another picture of the cheetah. Terms like "treatments" are used here to describe tourist interactions with animals.
Regardless, the experience itself remains at least questionable. If interactions supposedly follow only the animals' natural rhythms, it seems somewhat contradictory to visitors when fixed program points, clearly timed sequences, and very obviously staged moments are simultaneously part of the tour.
The flow already feels highly regulated, while visitors are mostly rushed from station to station in a short amount of time.
When animals are also clearly part of demonstrations, the question remains: where exactly is the line between experiencing the animals and the staged performance?
All in all, a disappointing experience, quite apart from the way tourists are treated here!

content:
In November, we had the opportunity to visit Cheetah’s Rock – an experience we won't soon forget. What was particularly moving was that we also got to meet the founder, Jenny, in person. Her warm, calm nature and the deep respect she shows the animals immediately impressed us.
Cheetah’s Rock is a recognized sanctuary for rescued animals – from rare white lions to Sykes' monkeys and lemurs, to otters and zebras, animals of all kinds and with diverse stories find a safe home here. The team works with incredible love, patience, and respect. Nothing is forced; every animal is free to retreat at any time.
If you're ever in Zanzibar, I highly recommend visiting Cheetah’s Rock and supporting this invaluable institution. For us, it was the absolute highlight of our vacation!
The visit is very informative and goes far beyond simply taking tourist photos. You learn a great deal about the animals' stories and the important work being done here. The animals' well-being is always the top priority, and the team consistently ensures that visitors behave respectfully. The animals appear well-cared for, calm, and friendly.
I'm not usually a fan of traditional zoos, but Cheetah's Rock is something completely different. The interactions here serve a clear purpose: Since veterinary care is difficult to access in Zanzibar and specialists often have to be flown in, it's crucial that the animals are regularly trained and can be examined without any problems. Many of them can no longer be released into the wild or come from poor living conditions – which makes the work done here all the more valuable. It's an aspect that might not be immediately apparent, but becomes very clear when you're there.
For us, it was an absolute 10/10 experience.

clauses.clause_text: Nothing is forced; every animal is free to retreat at any time.

In total, around €25 in fees just because I didn't have any cash. That's a rip-off! Especially nowadays and with such large sums!

You get closer to some of these animals than you probably ever will again in your life, which has an important reason behind it. There is no veterinary care for animals in Zanzibar. Therefore, it is essential that close contact is established between humans and animals on both sides.
You can feel the passion that goes into the project at every moment. It is very important to follow the staff's instructions. That's why it's really important to be able to speak English. The monkeys are quite playful and like to give "love bites." If you treat the animals respectfully and follow the instructions, you'll be fine. It was an incredible feeling to sit next to the cheetah, feed the bush babies, and pet the zebra. We will never forget the trip there and would highly recommend it to everyone. content:
BEWARE: If it feels wrong, it’s because it is. Here are the key elements that the owner won’t tell visitors.
1. CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) has absolutely no connection with ethical practices or animal wellbeing. It only control border movement of the animals.
2. ZIPA (Zanzibar Institute of Protected Areas) only ensures the bare minimum standards determined by Zanzibar, which are notably poor.
3. Research has proven time and time again physical interaction with wild animals generates stress and its detrimental to the animals health. Specially in felines where they spend long periods of time alone. This place provides no opportunity for the animal to retreat, a fundamental welfare issue.
Quoting research:
[Poor Welfare Indicators and Husbandry Practices at Lion (Panthera Leo) “Cub-Petting” Facilities, 2022]
[University of Oxford's Wildlife Conservation Research Unit]
4. The breeding programs combined with lion cub petting and walking are serious red flags of “Canned Hunting” pipelines. Where animals are bred and used while they are “cute” and harmless, later they are sold to private owners for hunting in private land.
In conclusion, while the desire to have a close encounter with a magnificent animal like a lion or cheetah is understandable, the evidence strongly suggests that facilities offering petting of large carnivores are overwhelmingly unethical.

Feeding and caring for all those animals... is a lot of work and definitely expensive. The experience itself. I don't want to spoil it for you... but you will learn a bit about animal training. You will learn about wildlife conservation in Africa. You will learn about a significant number of the animals there. You will learn about wildlife treatment on Zanzibar Island itself. And... you will definitely touch plenty of animals if you really like petting animals (I do). Not just mammals, either. You will also get to feed animals.
All of the trainers and people working the tour were very approachable, extremely serious about safety, and taught about or enforcing proper, ethical animal handling and treatment. I didn't want to participate in any unethical exploitation of animals and Cheetah's Rock treats all of its animals extremely ethically.

content:
Don’t let the critics put you off with complaints about the $160 entry fee. Yes, it’s more than your average attraction—but Cheetah’s Rock is far from average. This isn’t just a zoo. It’s a sanctuary where conservation experts dedicate their lives to rescuing, rehabilitating, and training animals with compassion and respect.
Every encounter is deeply educational. The team takes time to share insights about each animal and guide you on how to interact in a way that honors their wellbeing. If you’re a true animal lover, visiting a place where animals are respected—not exploited—is non-negotiable. And at Cheetah’s Rock, the care is exceptional.
I finally met my favorite animal—the cheetah—and I’m grateful I waited to do it here, rather than in a cage at some neglectful zoo. If you’re just after a quick selfie and not interested in the animals’ stories or the meaningful work behind the scenes, this place might not be for you. But if you want a heartfelt, ethical, and unforgettable animal experience, this is the paradise you’ve been looking for.

I visited Cheetah’s Rock yesterday, and I can say with all my heart – this place is one of a kind.The animals are not just cared for, they are protected, respected, and deeply understood by a team of experts who dedicate their lives to them.
What makes this place so different? The incredible closeness to the animals – done the right way. I have traveled a lot, but I have never seen anything like this. And the best part? You are not just a spectator. You learn, you connect, you understand.

I also read a review complaining about finances and transparency. That review is completely misleading. Cheetah’s Rock does NOT ask for donations. The entrance fee goes directly into the care and protection of the animals. And trust me – this is money well spent.

Cheetah’s Rock is not just a visit. It is an experience that changes the way you see wildlife.That’s why I am coming back for the VIP Otter Tour in some days – I simply cannot get enough of this place!

One important note for future visitors:
Please be careful when booking via “beach boys”:
Unfortunately, I was misled by a beach boy closely working with a taxi driver. He claimed to take me to Cheetah’s Rock after having taken the tour fee. Instead of driving me to Cheetah’s Rock, he dropped me at a completely different, unethical place and left. We found Cheetah's Rock through Google. Since I'm pregnant, we wanted to check via email first whether participation was possible for me. Communication via email was quick and easy. There were no obstacles to my participation; I only had to sign a separate form.
The pickup, which we booked, was flawless. Upon arrival, everyone was offered water and a coconut. Unfortunately, we noticed right away that some guests weren't following the rules explained by the rangers, which were available both online and in the car. For example, some were using sunscreen, which isn't good for the smaller animals.
The tour itself was very interesting. Plenty of time was taken to explain everything and each animal in detail, and there was also ample time for taking pictures. You could really feel the close bond between the rangers and the animals.
The explanations from Jenny, the founder, were also extremely interesting. She told us how the park came about, how it's financed, and much more.
For anyone who loves and appreciates animals, this excursion is perfect.
I do have one small suggestion for improvement, though: perhaps you could incorporate shorter water breaks along the way. Drinking is, of course, possible at any time, but it's outside the enclosures, and that means you miss some of the presentation.
Warm regards from Germany to the whole team! You're doing a fantastic job, and we'll definitely visit you again when we return to Zanzibar.

content:
You should support this!
You should see it!
I'm absolutely speechless. It was simply incredibly beautiful. I want to emphasize that all the animals are extremely well cared for, they have plenty of space, and the enclosures are designed to be very realistic. The whole team is doing a fantastic job. They told us so much about the animals: how they actually live, why each animal had to be taken in, and what the plan is for its future.
They put in a lot of work to prepare the animals so they can return to the wild. This takes a lot of time and money. Unfortunately, it's not possible for every animal. Sometimes the animal wouldn't be able to manage it, or, as with lions, because the authorities currently prohibit their release back into the wild. Nevertheless, they continue with the training. Firstly, because it takes years, and secondly, because the regulations can change again.
We swam with otters first. It was so much fun that I was laughing so hard I cried.
After that, a Maasai man took us to an incredibly beautiful spot: Arnoldis on the Cliff Bar and Bites. Beautiful and delicious.
We were allowed to spend two hours there.
Afterwards, we continued for four hours at Cheetah's Rock with the other rescued animals. It's often quite shocking to learn why these animals had to be taken in.
It's wonderful that such a place and such people exist who care so much for the animals.
None of the animals were forced to come to us. Those that wanted to come came, and some monkeys didn't, and that was just how it was. Of course, you're given food to attract the animals, but it's not like they starve them to make them come. They are all very well-fed. Also, they don't allow an unlimited number of visitors. For example, there were only two of us with the otters, and it's not an everyday occurrence.
You can tell that the animals' well-being is their top priority, but they can't help them any more without visitors.
It was one of the best days of my life, and I would recommend it to everyone. If I could, I would give it 100 stars.

content:
One of the most beautiful experiences of my life! At Cheetah's Rock, they rescue wild animals that have been mistreated, stolen from their mothers, and used for illegal purposes, animals rescued from zoos, or animals arriving from other contexts. Unfortunately, almost none of these animals can be released into the wild due to contact with humans or the impossibility of safely reintroducing them into their natural environment. All the animals in the reserve are respected, loved by their caregivers, and are free-roaming, vaccinated, and healthy.
For each animal, their story is told and the journey they took to arrive at this reserve.
It's important to visit this center, as it is self-financed through our visits. I absolutely recommend visiting Cheetah's Rock if you're in Zanzibar.
Thanks to everyone who works at Cheetah's Rock for their commitment to saving less fortunate animals!

content:
One of the highlights of our vacation!
The people were very friendly and shared a lot of stories about the animals. The founder herself was also there for a Q&A session and with the zebra, answering all questions thoroughly and providing additional information. You can tell that everyone is passionate about what they do and wants to give the animals the best possible life under the circumstances.
We were able to let the bush babies, monkeys, and lemurs jump all over us and feed them, and we even petted a cheetah and the zebra. The animals were free to move away at any time, and with the monkeys, you simply stayed seated, and they would approach you on their own (sometimes with the help of food). They clearly explain beforehand what you are allowed/supposed to do and what you aren't, and you can always say if you don't want to go near a particular animal. You feel well taken care of, and even during the cheetah encounter, there was only a little nervousness, more like excitement.
At first glance, the tour seems a bit expensive, but you experience something truly unique and support a worthwhile project at the same time.
For animal lovers, this is a must-see in Zanzibar!

content: We really enjoyed our stay at Cheetah Rocks. We went on two different days because the combined tour was already fully booked. But we don't regret it at all and would do it again in a heartbeat! On the Great Wildlife Tour, we were in a larger group and received precise instructions about what we could and couldn't do. I appreciate that the animals can always retreat if things get too overwhelming for them. We experienced so many animals up close: bush babies, monkeys, lemurs, and even the white lions and the tiger made an appearance. A dream came true for me when it was Latifa's turn and we were allowed to take photos with her. And I'd also like to mention that she could have left at any time if she had wanted to, so I don't think it's animal cruelty or profiteering. After all, their livelihood has to be financed somehow. Meat is expensive, and the vet costs money too. Jenny then introduced us to Beppo. She's simply a wonderful, genuine, and animal-loving person. On our second visit, we did the VIP Otter Experience. What was the advantage? No groups, just my husband, me, and the otters! JJ explained everything to us, and we learned a lot about otters—that they're cute but can also be quite different. Then it started, and we got to splash around with the otters and feed them. I was especially taken with Captain Jack, the sweet little one; I hope everything went well with the introduction to his new companion. And when we said goodbye to the otters, JJ said he'd like to introduce us to someone else he hadn't been able to show us the day before… and voilà, we got to visit a cheetah again and brush and pet it! I don't know how it's spelled (Sharqui?). We also received so much information about the different animals, and of course, there were many sad stories too! But now they're in loving hands and will be well cared for. Thank you all for your wonderful work. ❤️

content:
I must admit, the first time I saw this place online when researching our family trip to Zanizbar I was skeptical, but goodness me, how pleased I was to be proved so wrong. These animals are so incredibly cared for, all of the training they are given is not for entertainment but enrichment and ensures easier, less stressful administration of medical needs. The care that the owner and her wonderful team have, including Charlie & JJ for these animals is so evident.
For my Mum's birthday I purchased the otter experience. It was quite simply incredible. Our guide and keeper was Charlie, who was not only lovely, but so informative and he loved those otters so much, and it was evident that they adored him right back. He is the father of otters!!
As a full family we did the full tour today, something that we will never forget. Being able to stroke a cheetah, have lemurs and monkeys bounce onto your shoulders, bush babies crawl into your lap and even meet their newest resident Zebra for a neck scratch..... wow!!
It is so clear how cared for these animals are, they run on only positive reinforcements (mainly food) and each of the interactions are always on the animals terms (the primates have to choose to jump on you!) The rest are free to leave from the people if they wish and return to their enclosures.
You hear so many horror stories as an animal lover of drugged animals, declawed cats etc and Cheetahs Rock couldn't be further from this. It is truly a place where the animals are cherished and rescued from often awful situations, working with all the relevant authorities to ensure rare species conservation, rescue lions from apartment buildings when kept as pets etc.....
If you're on the fence, do it. As a proud animal lover with a massive interest in animal welfare, I can say it was one of the most amazing things I've ever done. Well done Jenny and team; and thank you for all that you do.

content: These people do such beautiful work. My compliments on the energy and passion they put into it. Absolutely worth visiting. It is unforgettable.

content: It's a pretty cool place, and you can tell they treat the animals with love. They're all friendly, very clean, and well-cared for. The only sad thing is that despite the excellent care, it's simply a money-making operation. The price seems out of this world... $160 to see five species of animals is really too much. The tour lasts four hours and involves listening to the animals (5-6 species) for the most part. I think the high price is solely based on the opportunity to take a photo with a cheetah. If you have the money, you can see it, but I personally wouldn't go back.

clauses.clause_text: $160 to see five species of animals is really too much.
