content:
We were there yesterday and it was simply fantastic. We were allowed to interact with the animals and received a lot of information from the animal keepers. Everyone was incredibly friendly and tried to include everyone. The animals are treated wonderfully and always get fresh food. Of course, they were attracted by the food; otherwise, they wouldn't have come, if you think about it logically. And if they didn't want to, they weren't forced. You can really tell that they love their animals; none of them were pushy about donations or extra money. It was worth every penny we paid. The owner is from Swabia, and you can see in her eyes how passionate she is about it. It was simply a delight, and it made us even more eager to go on a safari. And for people who don't have the money for a safari, it's a great alternative to see the animals.
As for the bad reviews, I can't understand them because it's not a so-called circus or a rip-off. Most of the money goes towards the animals' welfare. The owner definitely doesn't get rich from it, except for the joy it brings her. But they and the employees also have to live, so please don't write judgments here with your eyes closed, and that was putting it nicely.

clauses.clause_text: And if they didn't want to, they weren't forced.

content: The experience is too long and you feel bored after a while. The price is a little high as well as the kind of experience you get. The highlight is the cheetah of course but at some point you feel that it's a pet and not a wild animal. For some people this is sort of staged! The initiative is great but for me it should be cut in half as a time. Basically it's just feeding animals and listening to the experiences guides.

clauses.clause_text: The experience is too long and you feel bored after a while.

content:
We were here yesterday for the wildlife tour and we were absolutely thrilled!
You get picked up from your hotel and dropped off again – completely free of charge.
We received a super friendly welcome and were offered something to drink as soon as we arrived.
The staff were all incredibly helpful and approachable, knowledgeable about their animals, and their love and connection to them were immediately apparent.
We had plenty of time at each location, and the staff even took photos with their phones! Elsewhere, you pay an extra €15 for a single photo and are rushed off so quickly that you don't even have a chance to connect with the animals.
This money was 100% well spent, and you're also doing something good! For such a cause, it's even a bargain in my opinion.
Humans can be so cruel, and the stories about these animals are all heartbreaking – which makes us all the more grateful that there are still people like Jenny and her team who are working every day to regain the trust of these animals!
Keep up the great work, and thank you so much for this incredible experience! We'll remember this for a long time!!
Laura and Patrick

content:
Despite what the detractors of this exceptional place might say, we absolutely loved our experience at this rescue center.
Of course, it's important to understand the center's educational and dedicated mission. Yes, the animals are in cages, but most of them are endangered, and the goal is to preserve them and try to breed them in the best possible conditions.
As for the other animals, they were rescued from deplorable conditions (mistreatment, destined for the pet trade or to be eaten in certain restaurants).
So, yes, hats off to the work done by these truly passionate people who share their love for animals and the essential respect they deserve. 😃👍🏻

content:

The cheekier of the cubs (Marek or something like that?) playfully nipped me in the ribs, and I was as proud as punch of the little scar afterward. Sadly, it's faded.
I definitely got the impression that the animals were well cared for, and for us human visitors, it was unforgettable.
Sure, it's quite an expensive activity for an afternoon, but it was definitely worth it – and the animals can't exactly pay for their own food.
So, thank you and best regards to Jenny and the team, and also to the son, who I'm sure has become a great tiger tamer!

We found this disappointing for the high price, as half a minute isn't enough to truly appreciate such an extraordinary moment (with the cheetah). The contact with other animals, like monkeys, bush babies, and the zebra, is significantly longer. The group size also struck us as a drawback. This was mainly because some visitors, in their quest for the best photo, showed no consideration and pushed their way to the front. If everyone were more mindful of each other, the number of participants wouldn't be such a problem. Overall, however, it's a wonderful and beautifully designed place that provides the animals with a safe haven. Definitely worth a visit, but the cheetah encounters are very brief.

content:
We visited Cheetah's Rock yesterday and we are overwhelmed.
It was the absolute highlight of our vacation.
It's wonderful to see that there are still people like those at Cheetah's Rock who aren't just in it for the money.
The animals are treated with such respect and love. In my opinion, it's precisely this respectful and loving approach that allows you to get closer to the animals than anywhere else. The team on site does an outstanding job and commands my utmost respect!
We are absolutely blown away! I love nature and animals, and I prefer to explore them "by chance" and leave them in peace. Just observe, enjoy the experience, and then move on. With the bushbabies, for example, it was lovely to see that when one of them retreated, it was truly left alone. Here, the animals can still decide for themselves whether and how intensely they want to interact.
Mario led this expedition with great professionalism and humor. It's clear that all the staff have a deep respect for the animals. It's wonderful to see that there are still places where animals are treated the way they deserve.
You gladly put up with the countless mosquito bites.
At some point, I didn't even want to take any more photos because I was so fascinated by everything and just wanted to observe.
The only "negative" point:
After this experience, we regret not booking the combined tour ;-).
All the best to Jenny, Mario, and all the staff at Cheetah's Rock for this extraordinary experience and the fantastic work they do here!
Best regards,
Markus & Christina Wollmann

content: On various forums you will find a lot of different discussions about this place. It is not my job to convince you of either side of the argument. For me, visiting this place was an amazing lifelong experience. It is worth being in a place where, in my opinion, animals are cared for with a big heart and their stories are told with passion. It doesn't matter if you go on safari to the mainland afterwards because it's a different experience. We were picked up by a car from Paje and driven to Cheetah's Rock. We took one person along the way. On the spot, we sign a statement that we will not blame the resort for any damage to health blown up by animals. Sounds serious but the crew cares about our safety very much and they have a lot of experience. During your stay at the resort, the staff makes sure that we take a picture with the animal ... we don't have to worry about it. During the four-hour stay, we will get to know the stories of our heroes, we will be able to touch most of them or feed and meet the amazing founder and her crew. The cost of the Great Wildlife Tour is USD 160. You can say it's a lot but remember that you are helping to keep these animals and besides, the safari costs several times more and you will never be as close to wild animals as in Cheetah's Rock.

content:
My husband and I booked a day-long excursion to this delightful animal sanctuary. In the morning, we enjoyed a private playtime with the otters. We got to provide enrichment time treats and stimulation while learning about their stories and the species as a whole. With some extra time remaining, we got to meet some of the big cats at the rescue privately. That was unforgettable!
In the afternoon, we got to meet several really cool animals. We fell in love with a white tigeress and chuffed with her mate. We got tiger kisses and scratched them behind the ears. The rescue is doing really great work here. Some amputees, some poacher rescues, some apartment pet rescues, some rehabs that will be released. Pretty impressive. Very clean. Very educational. The animal ambassadors are helping the rescue raise money. Yea, it was commercial, but for a good cause. The animals are not ever forced to perform on demand, and it is clear that their welfare takes top priority.
Thank you, Katerina and Danny and the whole staff at Cheetahs Rock for an unforgettable adventure.

We got very close to the animals, which was very interesting and exciting. However, we felt that the only goal was to get a great photo with all the different animals. The zebra performed tricks that are usually done with dogs, and the other animals were lured with food to sit on our shoulders so we could get a good picture. Some of the monkeys were aggressive, which is of course part of nature, but also dangerous. When we were with the lions, we sat like we were in a movie theater and were handed champagne. At the cheetah, we had to line up and could then sit next to it for the perfect photo and pet it.
We left the tour with a pretty bad feeling and would have preferred to stop, but it was very, very expensive!
We do believe that animal welfare and rescue are the primary concerns, but unfortunately, the animals were treated like a show, which is definitely not the point!

I'll start with the positive points.The booking procedure was smooth. They explain their prices clearly on their website. You can write to them on whatsapp and they answer quickly. Everyone was friendly and the employees make sure that you get a good picture with all animals.
It seems like the animals are well cared for. They mention that they have access to top vets in Austria, Italy, and South Africa. It was just the part about these lion cubs that made me feel uncomfortable and regret my trip.
This place was a lighter version of Tiger King. I started the visit hoping that I would be supporting someone who was providing a haven for animals that had nowhere else to go. I was on board for the story of most of the animals until we met Jenny, the founder of the park.
She explained that the female lion, a white lion of which none exist more in the island, Savanna recently had two cubs. A few days later, they realized there was a dead cub in the placenta and it was removed. The mother lion was in severe pain and incapable of caring for the living cubs.
Jenny said, 'The cubs are with me.'"

content:
I wish I could give negative stars to this place.
DO NOT WASTE time and money ON Cheetah Rock, there is so much more Zanzibar has to offer, this highly commercialized operation is not worth it.
Plus the owner is mentally unstable person who threatens anyone who dares to not love her place or making money.
This place (the owner in particular) portray themselves as animal lovers and Cheetah Rock as wild life caring place but in reality it’s a money making scheme that milks tourists and offers zoo/circus like photo opportunities.
Zebra trained to fetch and pick up and kick ball, monkeys eating pasta, etc. has nothing to do with wild life or care for wild animals.
They take a group of 40-50 people thru 1/2 dozen animal enclosures (pretty small ones at that) and spend most time for every tourist to take pictures. This experience takes 4 hours not because you see or experience much, but rather because it’s lengthy photo-op session, you see very little in reality.
The owner of the place offered lengthy and semi-hysterical lecture on how terrible humans are towards animals and how COVID was fake (because pandemic and decline in tourism obviously impacted her income stream).
We left the tour after 1.5 hours as it was both boring and offensive for anyone who likes wild life rather than Zoo-circus like experiences.
We did mention to the person who was fetching our car that we found experience both disappointing and overpriced. And in response the owner yelled in front of the whole group of 40 at hour daughter (who stayed behind with her friends) that we blackmailed her staff. Ridiculous!!!!
She clearly throws a fit and writes threatening responses for any non-positive review (checkout Tripadvisor reviews), including mine.
When I reached out to the place and requested an apology for such outrageous behaviour after our disappointing experience, they couldn’t care less and didn't bother to even respond.
Save yourself time and money while in Zanzibar, DO NOT WASTE IT ON Cheetah Rock. Zanzibar has so much real beauty and animal life to offer.

content:
This was one of our highlights in Zanzibar.
Can you really get close to the animals and touch them? YES! (except the big cats)
First we saw the Zebra which you could feed and play little games with. Wow.
Then we went to different kinds of monkeys which we were feeding from our hands. Some you could touch, some hop on your shoulder and hands. You can even touch the peacock sometimes.
Our last station was the big cats like tigers, lions and pumas. Those were of course behind a fence but still we were able to get really close to them. What an experience!
Lastly we were able to make photos with a cheetah and touch his hindside. This was awe inspiring and an amazing experience.
The staff always gave the backstory to the animals, told us what to look for and consider when getting close to them. We felt very well taken care of and instructed. They talk passionately about the animals and those look well fed and taken care of.
One more highlight was the talk with the founder who talked about the project, how the animals came to her and struggles she faced while building up the program. Such passion! Admirable.
All in all we had a great time, took nice pictures and now have impressions of a life time. It was well worth the money and we are glad that we visited this place.

content:

For animal lovers, it's a must-do experience!
Highly recommended.

Fruit juice or soda would have been much more appreciated! Charging 10,000 CFA francs per group visit seems absurd, knowing that fruits and vegetables here in Zanzibar cost almost nothing. Meat might be more expensive, admittedly, but I think it's a rip-off at that price! The best part is at the end when you get to enjoy the cheetah for three minutes! So, for French people who would like to do this, go for it; it's an extraordinary experience, but it's still expensive!

However, that doesn't justify everything. Here, they allow themselves to put on real shows to impress tourists. A poor zebra worked in a zoo, and Cheeta's Rock rescues him to play ball in front of forty or so tourists seated on a platform: it's a circus.

content: My opinion of the place is rather mixed. When I booked, I was expecting a magical and intimate experience with animals roaming almost freely (the enclosure was very large considering the price of the land). Upon arrival, I was very unpleasantly surprised by the size of the group for the day: about forty people. So much for the intimate atmosphere. We were immediately asked to sit in a sort of tent at the entrance, where a zebra entered to perform a show sadly reminiscent of Zavatta. We then found ourselves feeding nocturnal animals in broad daylight. A question about their missing teeth was quickly dismissed with a vague response. A puma was presented to us in a 2m² cage. We continued in this way, visiting enclosures whose size was highly questionable given the animals. The cause is obviously worthy, and the staff is very pleasant, hence the 3 stars, but the price seems far too high considering the conditions and the circus/show atmosphere I experienced. I would like to clarify that I am not particularly involved in animal rights activism.

content:
We are so glad we found out about this! Yes, it's pricy experience, but you for sure see where the money goes - directly for the animal care. We had so much fun here and we learned plenty of interesting stuff.
Only thing that was a bit annoying - there are too many people on the tour at the same time (about 35-40 on ours) and it gets really crowded, you barely get opportunity to meet the animals by yourself, because some people just won't let you. I'd say 20 should be the max.
However! Where else you get the chance to see such rare animals as the white lion, golden tiger or angonoka/plougshare tortoise? There are just few left in the wild.
If you have the chance, visit this place and see for yourself.
Mind you, this is not your regular petting zoo. If the animal doesn't want to be touched, you have to respect it.
But still - I pet a zebra, got my head jumped on by bushbabies and monkeys, lemurs, saw dikdiks, pet a rare tortoise, gave an apple to striped hyena, touched the cheetah and tiger (!).
Was it worth it? Absolutely.

During the tour, you learn about the different animals and why they're there. Some of the stories are sad and terrible. The owner, Jenny, even took a few minutes to talk to us, even though she had to take care of the lion cubs during our visit.

content:
We had a very exceptional experience at Cheetah's Rock. First, I can confirm all the good reviews for this place: The team cares a lot about every single animal and they are doing whatever is possible to ensure a good life for them. Sure, it is stunning to get in close contact with these animals, but what is even more important is to see that there is a lovely place for animals which can not be released to the wild anymore. With your entry fee, you will definitely save lives!
But now I want to explain why our visit was something special.
The plan to visit Africa and to go on a safari was our dream for a long time. My girlfriend's favorite animal is the zebra, and she was so lucky when we finally booked the trip to Tanzania. What she didn't know was that I already got in contact with Jenny and the Cheetahs Rock Team for an unusual request.
When I found out about Cheetah's Rock and visited the website, the first thing that jumped into my eyes was Chaka with a rose in his mouth. Chaka is probably the best trained zebra on earth and he can do a lot of tricks. So I contacted Jenny to ask her if she can train Chaka to give a rose to my girlfriend. Not a normal rose but a rose with an engagement ring! Jenny and the team were so kind and tried everything to make this happen. They also did additional training sessions with Chaka to make sure everything will work out perfectly.
When we finally visited Cheetah's Rock I was so nervous as I knew: “If this will work, it will be the perfect proposal for her”. And in the end everything was working flawlessly. Chaka did a great job and my fiancee was overwhelmed! This day will be forever in our memories.
Thank you Jenny, thank you dear Cheetah's Rock Team for everything. Not only for this one moment but for an unforgettable day. And last but not least: Thank you Chaka, you are the GOAT.
We wish you the very best for the future.

clauses.clause_text: When I found out about Cheetah's Rock and visited the website, the first thing that jumped into my eyes was Chaka with a rose in his mouth.

After all, you are paying £160pp. The other thing I didn’t like is how many people are squeezed into the experience. You are put with 40 other people and can barely fit into most of the enclosures which should be a sign they need to reduce numbers. The zebra bit felt a bit circus like too.

content:

I was also lucky with my group, everyone understood that the animal dictates interraction. Animals come first even in these difficult times, which is very nice to see. We also took advantage of the comfortable and spatious taxi ride from Stonetown to the resque and then to our next stop saving on transportation cost and with a good driver. content:
This is a nice place to see different exotic animals up close but if you are expecting a lot of interaction than you are at the wrong place!
Here they like to talk about the animal, it's sad story and the species struggles in the wilderness. So if you are an animal fanatic and really interested in facts than this is the place.
Furthermore this place is extremely commercial which is a big disappointment: the price is very high just to see animals an hear their long stories. Their tours are also made of about 40 people so when you finally get the chance to touch an animal you only have about one second.
I've visited a number of other animal rescues in Africa that were way better: less commercial, a lot more natural and with a lot more interaction.
I've gone home with mixed feelings after my visit and hope this review will help someone!

Animals - folks, let me tell you, you get up close and personal with the animals. From monkeys, lemurs to Cheetah’s and tigers. The experience was surreal. You really get to learn about the history of the animal and how they were rescued and re-homed in a nourishing environment.
The staff - The staff are incredibly professional, welcoming and definitely kept us entertained. They made sure that our safety was a priority and kept us briefed throughout. Very impressed with the service.
Price - at first, it might seem like the tour is expensive but it was all worth the money. Once you see the effort and funding that goes into creating this experience, it’s a small price to pay.
In conclusion, if you’re visiting Zanzibar and if you’re an animal lover, this is a must do activity. Highly recommended. 🙂

content:
This was an excellent experience that I would highly recommend if you have some free time in Zanzibar. First, I want to say that this is a TRUE animal sanctuary through and through (based on the research I did before visiting and also everything I observed while there.) I have visited other rescues in other parts of the world that because of political or economic pressure, have made certain compromises to stay open and be able to maintain operations, but at some expense to their animals. In the situations they are in, they reason that the animals are at least better off there than where they were before (and usually they are), but they have to make their location more lucrative in order to stay afloat. At Cheetah’s Rock, I didn’t witness any such compromise. Their policies always appeared to put animal welfare and visitor safety over gimmick-y tourist attractions (which is much rarer than you would think!), while still maintaining an enjoyable and educational experience for visitors. For example, once lions reach maturity (they are much more aggressive than cheetahs when fully grown), they no longer allow photos with visitors- which is the safest and most humane thing! —
For a more detailed account:
A round trip driver to and from your hotel (for most areas on the island) is included in the price. Our driver was on time, courteous, and got me excited for the visit. Upon arrival, our guide, Shane, was very welcoming and told us what we could expect, briefed us on safety procedures, and was very up front about any risks with specific animals and experiences. It was raining when we arrived, so we started under a covered area, where we met an adorable zebra, Chaka. We were told how staff only use positive reinforcement to build trust in the animals, which not only allow visitors to interact, but more importantly, allow vets to treat the animals without using tranquilizing drugs for routine check-ups, which is much healthier. Then we met a gorgeous puma (who was in heat!) and were told her heartbreaking story before being rescued. We then got to go into an enclosure with some lemurs, who we could feed as they sat on our shoulders, and one of the rarest species in the world, Ploughshare Tortoises!! We also visited a psyches blue monkey and two playful vervets. One of my favorite encounters was with the bush babies! The are super interested in you- sniffing you, preening your hair and giving you lots of love. Then, we were served champagne and refreshments before meeting Aslan the lion! He stays in his enclosure for safety, BUT, volunteers who would rise to the challenges can start by making eye contact, leading to a race up and down the grounds. I volunteered and it was so cool to connect with this lion and get him excited to race, switching back and changing direction while maintaining eye contact. We later saw some beautiful and very rare golden tabby tigers. Finally, of course, we were able to pose with the cheetahs. There were two separate cheetah encounters, both allowing photo opportunities.
The only advice I would give is that someone in your group take your pictures (allowed only for the first cheetah encounter). I was a solo traveler so relied on the staff to take pictures and unfortunately did not get a single usable picture with the cheetahs (almost all were blurry or the cheetah was cut out of the frame). But, the couple that was in my car took their own photos and were very satisfied with theirs (and were a little more pushy with getting photo time). If I went again, I would just have another guest take my pictures☺️. On the second cheetah encounter, our group was a bit time pressured and because of the rain, the sunlight was gone, but we were still able to get very close to an even bigger cheetah and learn about why some were named after the royal family in Dubai. We later saw the adorable otters when passing outside their “night house”.
Thank you Cheetah’s Rock for maintaining your integrity and staying true to your mission❤️❤️

I was a solo traveler so relied on the staff to take pictures and unfortunately did not get a single usable picture with the cheetahs (almost all were blurry or the cheetah was cut out of the frame).

content:
We started our experience at Cheetah's Rock on the first day with the VIP Otter Experience. It was such a wonderful and amazing experience to feed the little Otter pirates and play in the water with these lively and joyful animals, which were full of energy. They made us smile the full time, we immediately fell in love with Bloody Mary, Cpt. Hook, Cpt. Blackbeard and Cpt. Jack Sparrow. There won’t be any other way than to fully enjoy this encounter. We are recommending the program to everyone. A big thank you as well for Leaveil and Stephan who made us feel very comfortable. They did a fantastic job, they were very kind, friendly, also took pictures about us and the animals and could always answer our questions. They ensured that the animals were always looked after while we (and they) played with them. This created a very pleasant atmosphere.
The Great Wildlife Experience took place on the next day. The tour starts with a welcome coconut water and a mandatory briefing. From the beginning you could see with what dedication, love and passion the employees in Cheetah‘s Rock look after the animals. Their well-being always comes first and is their top priority. They are making no profits out of the tours, all the money goes directly to the animals and helps the team sustain their operations. They are not getting any support from the government, that’s why the entrance fee for such an experience is more than justified. We learned a lot about their vision and goals and about the current situation concerning the flora and fauna in Zanzibar. That’s why their conservation work is even more important. From the staff we learned a lot about the animals at Cheetah‘s Rock. About their species but especially about their individual, mostly very sad back story. The most of the animals are rescued and adopted and due to ongoing physical impairments they will never be released to the wild as it would mean their certain death. At Cheetah‘s Rock they can live a happy, sheltered life in a large and spacious enclosure, which is adapted to their natural habitat. With so many different wild animals living in one place it is of course necessary to have fence between the different enclosures as a safety restraint. The resident Zoologist Stephan had a great deal of knowledge and could answer all the visitor questions in detail. The same applies for Leaveil and the rest of the employees, who led the group through the afternoon in a well-structured manner.
One of the highlights of course was the interaction with the different animals. This was again an experience for a lifetime. For example the soccer play with the zebra stallion Chaka, or having the opportunity to sit beside the cheetah Maktoum and touch him. Or feeding the bush babies, lemurs or monkeys treats while they are jumping from shoulder to shoulder, or helping the white lion Aslan having his 10kg meat per day, while having a refreshment for yourself with sparkling wine or water. It is very nice to see what a great deal of trust there is between the trainers and the animals, which is transferred to the visitors. For example the zebra stallion Chaka is trained to loose its fear of people and to build trust in order to get medical care. That is very important because at Cheetah‘s Rock the animals are not declawed, defanged, drugged in order to treat them nor forced to do anything by force. The interaction with the trainer or the visitors also enriches their lives so that they do not get bored.
We definitely recommend visiting Cheetah‘s Rock and if it’s possible to book both available programs. You do not only get educated very well, you also get the opportunity to get very close to a lot of wild animals, to touch and feed them, which leaves you with a breathtaking feeling. At Cheetah‘s Rock they mediate perfect consciousness for wildlife conservation. Your visit will not only enrich your, but also the animals life. A big thank you to the staff for making it an unforgettable experience and providing us two of the best days of our lives.
Kinga & Benedikt

content:
It all goes down to your expectations and why you’re here.
If you’re here because of your love for animals, then you came to the right place. If you’re here because of the good cause of protecting endangered animals, then you’re definitely in the right place. But if you’re here to have sufficient time interacting one-on-one with the big cats, then you’ll likely be disappointed.
Here’s the itinerary:
1)) you arrive and get welcomed with fresh coconut water.
2)) you wait for everybody else to arrive, approximately 30 in total
3)) you get briefed for an hour about safety procedures, their mission, global climate etc. by an enthusiast that you’d enjoy listening to.
4)) you start with a Zebra interaction (feeding, playing with and petting) that takes about an hour, feels childish but yet entertaining.
5)) you move to Bush Monkeys interaction then to Lemur (so-called Lima Monkey), then to Dik-Dik, then to a rare specie of tortoises and peacocks. You get to see also a gorgeous rescued Cougar in a cage. That’s another 2 hours of feeding and petting.
6)) here comes the long waited gorgeous majestic 5 years old white lion. Of course you get to learn about it and see it from behind the cage. You get to feed it from behind the cage too.
7)) then you’re walked and briefed from behind the cage while they feed two cubs a Liger and a Tiger. Both are breathtakingly beautiful.
8)) this is followed by a photo shoot with two beautiful Cheetahs inside their enclosure but without any interaction more than petting its back while being photographed for few seconds, for the next in turn to do the same.
9)) lastly you’re surprised by meeting two young cubs (lion and tiger) who got walked on a leash separately to get close to the audience to pet their back as they swiftly walk past them.
Personally I feel like every one-on-one interaction is rushed due to the large number of the audience from start to finish. And especially when it comes to the big cats, I feel I left Cheetah’s Rock longing for more than what I got. I was told there’s a VIP experience that provides that, but personally I didn’t know about it, and even if I did I’d not have known what to expect from the original one verses the VIP one. Therefore I hope my review helps future visitors to decide.

The zebra was treated like it was in a circus and had to perform tricks. I don't feel the animals were mistreated at all, but well, I still didn't feel good about it. We visitors were given the impression that we shouldn't be there, that they only run the tours to make money: period. Animal welfare comes before human well-being. This was emphasized more than once. I had wanted to fulfill my dream of touching a cheetah. Unfortunately, I was unlucky and was (luckily only lightly!) nipped on the knee by one of the two leopards roaming around. I panicked so much, I didn't know if I could say anything without provoking the animal. Luckily, it left me alone. That was enough for one day. The day was very tiring; the highlight was the lemurs and bush babies. At least you were allowed to pet them, even if it was very chaotic due to the large number of visitors. I would I wouldn't recommend anyone go there. It's better to donate the money; that will help the animals more.

content: It's a petting zoo. You go into cages, sit down, and then they let tame animals into your cage. You can feed them (they give you something to eat), touch them, and take photos. We fed a lion in a cage and gave him meat. The lion was adorable, petted and well-fed, and the video shows he's very friendly with people. At the end of the tour, they give you champagne. What I didn't like: there were a lot of people, and the presenter talks a lot, A LOT, A LOT! It just got tiresome. It's worth a one-time visit! A photo hugging a tame cheetah outdoors, an indri on your shoulder, galagos everywhere—well, it's Africa!

You can experience the animals up close, and they're really well cared for.

content:
Forodhani Park in Stone Town is where the evening comes to life. It's hot and quiet during the day, but everything changes as the sun sets. Stalls appear out of nowhere, smoke from barbecues hangs in the air, and the smell of seafood, spices, and juices fills the air.
The key is to take your time. Just wander around, choosing what to try. Squid, octopus, shrimp, Zanzibar pizza, fresh sugarcane juice. People are smiling, bargaining, and joking. The atmosphere is light, warm, a little chaotic, but cozy in its own way.
If you want to experience the real Stone Town, go there in the evening. It's not just food; it's a slice of island life.

clauses.clause_text: Stalls appear out of nowhere, smoke from barbecues hangs in the air, and the smell of seafood, spices, and juices fills the air.

content:

I couldn't speak English at all, and they quoted me a high price in dollars, so I was glad I had Tanzanian shillings! 🤣
We ordered juice, grilled food, and the famous Zanzibar pizza! 🍕💕
By the way, the grilled food, bananas, and rice balls were terrible. The seafood was delicious, though, mainly because of the atmosphere. 😋 While we were eating, a swarm of cats gathered around us – there were so many, it was surprising! 😂

content:
Out of all the experiences in Zanzibar, this one was my favourite.
It was my first time zip-lining, and no better place to do it than in the land of your descendants.
I was with my family, and we ran into the director whilst we were there. They shared what it took to bring this experience to life in Zanzibar and what their visions are going forward. Greatly appreciate them sharing their insights.
The members of the team who took us through the forest were also so friendly and informative. One of my family members was imploring them to make it known that “this is the world’s LONGEST single span zip line in East Africa”.
It was incredibly beautiful to see a part of Zanzibar from above, but walking through it was also curative.
There are several trails, some of which are a little difficult, but the plants and animals will make you overlook this and propel you to challenge yourself.
I would do it all over again.
There were quite a few things under construction, e.g. restaurant, zip line end, etc., when I was there, so hopefully when I return, it’ll be good to see the new additions and enhancements.
Please DO NOT build the viewpoint, I personally don’t think it’s necessary. From where we were standing, it was a sufficient view (less is more in this case).

content:
Very nice location in the middle of the beach and good friendly and laid back school manager and teachers. Joao did a great job and was patient with us. Prices are steep though. Had lots of fun and great experience overall.
One thing I’d like to point out is that the school or rather the instructors should ensure that if you pay for two hours’ tuition, you actually get two hours of active instruction. We actually started lessons late on a regular basis – partly due to preparations, choosing the right kite and walking to the training spot, or simply because everything moved at a slower pace and last time I checked we literally started the lesson with a 15 min delay (which is totally fine, as it’s all ‘pole pole’ and ofc preparations are also part of the learning), but we’d then finish early and were, so to speak, already out of the water before the end of the two hours, meaning you effectively only had 1.5 hours of lessons (sometimes it felt like just one hour). I understand that other people might have a lesson session afterwards, but in future it should be planned a bit more efficiently.

content:
Great school, kind people and high quality equipment.
If you want to learn kitesurfing, this is the right place. The staff is professional, friendly and always happy to give useful advice, even when renting on your own. The team is made up of both locals and instructors from all over the world, so you will easily find someone who speaks your language, which is a real advantage during lessons.
The equipment is in excellent condition and clearly separated between lessons and rental.
I was supposed to stay in Zanzibar for just one week, but once I discovered how good kitesurfing was, I decided to stay for a month to really learn properly. It’s a challenge with yourself that is worth every hour spent improving. A true form of therapy.
I arrived in Zanzibar after a difficult period, and thanks to kitesurfing I feel much better now. Part of the credit goes to this place, but above all to the people. Leaving is truly hard: here I found friends, not just instructors.
Thank you from the heart to all of you. For the kite, the support and the atmosphere you created.

content:
Unbiased, honest review after spending 7 days here: Kite Center Zanzibar is hands down THE BEST KITESURFING CENTER in all of Paje! 😊 WE ABSOLUTELY LOVED SPENDING OUR DAYS HERE!
My friends and I came to Zanzibar on a 7-day holiday to do kitesurfing. We did a lot of research before hand and decided we will be using Kite Center Zanzibar as our preferred choice throughout our stay. Little did we know, this was the best decision we have made throughout this trip! Even after arriving to Zanzibar, on our first day we went to check out multiple schools on the beach (B4, Aquaholics, and several others). However, none were as friendly and accommodating as the team over at Kite Center Zanzibar.
We were first greeted by Stephanie! Who is super friendly, always smiling and easy going - an absolute pleasure to deal with! She explained to us all details about the spot, entry point to the lagoon, location of the reef, areas with seaweed farms (a place you should not go to during low tide), and all other aspects of where to ride in the lagoon. She also gave us a walk around the center and where all facilities were. We later met Baris whom we were also dealing with on daily basis and he was very kind and friendly with all our requests and inquiries. The crew on the ground helping us out (especially Saeed) were super kind and looking out for us all the time!
My friend and I know how to kite so we brought our gears with us. We rented a locker for the entirety of the week and it was brand new and clean. Felt very safe keeping our gear there.
Our 3rd friend is new to kitesurfing so he took the beginner course with their team members and absolutely loved it. They have very clean, well maintained equipment for students (walkie talkie, helmets, vests, etc). My other friend also took a 1-hour advanced lesson with Coach Mohammed to learn transition and he managed to do it from the first trial!! Absolutely brilliant! 😁
I personally rented a 17m kite on the days with low wind and it was in great condition!
Honestly, this was our first time in Zanzibar and it was such an unforgettable experience, mainly because we spent a great deal of time (most of our mornings) at Kite Center Zanzibar with Baris, Stephanie and the rest of the team!! We loved it so much that we wanted to extend a few more days but we had to return home for work :( - Next time inshAllah!

content:
**Review for Kite Centre Zanzibar**
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
I recently had the most incredible experience at Kite Centre Zanzibar, and I can't praise the staff enough! From the moment I arrived, I was greeted with warmth and friendliness that instantly made me feel at home. The entire team was not only professional but also incredibly flexible and accommodating, making sure every aspect of my visit was tailored to my needs. They are IKO affiliated and it shows.
My instructor, Mo, was simply awesome! He struck the perfect balance between expertise and friendliness instilling confidence in me right from the start. His knowledgeable guidance made learning to kite surf enjoyable and stress-free. Mo took the time to understand my skill level and tailored our 3 sessions perfectly, ensuring I progressed at a comfortable pace. He was a perfect match for me and I suspect the same for most new or relatively new kite surfers.
Zanzibar itself offers the perfect conditions for learning kite surfing, with its consistent winds and stunning turquoise waters creating an ideal environment for both beginners and experienced kite surfers alike. The amazing scenery only added to the overall experience, making it truly unforgettable.
The combination of the incredible location and the fantastic staff made my time at Kite Centre Zanzibar exceptional. I highly recommend this place to anyone looking to experience kite surfing. Kudos to Mo and the entire Kite Centre team for an unforgettable adventure!

content: It started with us arriving at the kite centre and finding that no one there had taken our first day of lessons into account. So, someone had to be rounded up immediately so we could start a relatively expensive course (after later asking locals for prices and searching at kite schools in the Netherlands). We had never kited before and received no theoretical explanation whatsoever, nor did anyone warn us about the severe risk of sunburn here (even though the owners are Dutch). It was very annoying, because I still had to go into the water for another two days after that. Now, two months later, those severe sunburns are still visible (and yes, I did apply sunscreen and wore a t-shirt). No one was willing to help at any point. This also became apparent when I was forced to buy a long-sleeved shirt in their shop for €60. Even then, they wouldn't help me properly in the shop, as is customary in a store. Especially a shop like this at a dive school. After almost a week in Paje, we ran into the owners regularly, and while we said 'hi,' they didn't say a word. I see few bad reviews otherwise, so perhaps we just had bad luck with various things. Maybe we had a bad week with setbacks? We didn't speak to anyone anymore and just quietly finished our kite course. That was fine otherwise, and the equipment was good too.

You can kite at both high and low tide.
Strangely, we had bad weather at the beginning of January and didn't always get out.
We always used sails:
-13-15 for the lightest ones
-15-19 for the heaviest in the group
In any case, the sea and spot are highly recommended.
They prefer cash payment, as otherwise they charge an additional 3% commission.

content: I went to Zanzibar for a week to learn kite surfing. I had my eyes already on this school but hadn't pre-booked anything. When I arrived in Paje, I just walked in and was welcomed very warmly. The staff is very friendly, relaxed and flexible. They ran me through my options and I ended up taking 2-hours sessions every day for 5 days. It was my first-time kite surfing and I didn't know what to expect really. My instructor put a lot of emphasis on making me feel comfortable and safe and adjusted the sessions to my learning speed. Once I managed the water start, they installed a walkie talkie on my helmet so that I could stay in touch with my instructor which gave me a lot of reassurance. I had lots of fun in the water and it's a nice feeling if someone guides you while slowly becoming more independent and cheers for you through a mic for each of your small successes. In terms of bookings and payment - you can book your sessions for the next day after your session. They will recommend you the times depending on your level, the tides and the expected weather conditions - so the more flexibility you have the better. Payment can be done via card (5% surcharge like all of Zanzibar apart from Stonetown) and cash. The school is Dutch hence you might want to find out if you can do bank transfer to a Euro account. If you are new to water sport, they also run a small shop where you get the right water wear for your experience.

content:
Matemwe Beach is probably one of the most beautiful beaches on all of Zanzibar, comparable to the northern beaches and the area around Mnemba Island. The turquoise water and white sand are truly stunning.
Unfortunately, there is a significant problem with plastic waste. Large amounts of trash can be found on the beach, and the locals do not seem to care much about it. We tried to clean up some of it ourselves but eventually stopped when we noticed that holes are dug in the sand at night to bury the garbage. Additionally, during high tide, a river further north appears to be used to flush the village’s waste directly into the ocean.
Another downside is the constant presence of sellers. While they are generally friendly, they are extremely persistent and quickly become exhausting.
You should urgently pay attention to low and high tide. Otherwise, it is sometimes not possible — or even dangerous — to enter the water. In addition, you should expect sea urchins.
Zanzibar has incredible natural beauty, but the local population still has a lot to learn when it comes to environmental protection and respectful interaction with tourists.

The reef is mostly dead, and the only reason we saw a lot of colorful fish was because the guides were feeding them, which I consider to be really unethical. People were stepping on the reef, partly because the water was too shallow. We told the guide we weren’t interested in trying to find dolphins as we weren’t interested in chasing them.

I know that local people are just trying to make a living, but it’s so unfortunate that the government of Tanzania doesn’t care enough to regulate tourism so that the reef will be protected for the future.

content:
We booked the trip to Pengume Island and the dolphin swim with Rafiki Tours.
We booked through Instagram and paid via PayPal, which was very convenient and trustworthy!
We were picked up promptly at the agreed time and headed straight to the dolphins, which weren't far away.
There were about 10 boats with tourists there, which made us feel a bit like hunters. We had a private boat to ourselves, which was very nice.
Snorkeling mask, mask, and fins were provided, although I would recommend bringing your own equipment.
Since the dolphins are very fast, swimming with them was rather hectic: the boat comes close, you jump into the sea with your gear, watch the dolphins swim past you for about 30 seconds, and then have to climb back onto the boat (relatively tiring, even for young people). This process is repeated until you say you want to stop.
It's also worth mentioning that no life jackets were provided, which was the case with other tour operators.
After that, we went back to the shore and loaded tables, chairs, and provisions. Then we went to the mangroves near Pengume Island and even saw two monkeys. Next, we went to a snorkeling spot: however, all the coral was dead, and only a few fish were visible. This spot was frequented by several boats, meaning it was operated by other companies.
Afterward, we went to a place where we could see starfish. Then we went to a sandbar with stunningly beautiful blue water, where we were treated to delicious grilled seafood and other treats.
Afterward, we were dropped off by boat at our hotel, as it was low tide. All in all, a fantastic excursion, and booking directly was about €30 cheaper at €80 per person than booking through the hotel reception.
Furthermore, the two captains were very friendly and accommodating. 100% recommended.

content:
I want to warn other travelers about this experience.
We specifically chose this tour because we were told that snorkeling would be the main activity. We also made it clear that we did not want to see dolphins, as we strongly disagree with the way dolphins are chased by tourist boats in Zanzibar.
Despite this, our guide took us straight to the dolphins. What we witnessed was shocking: around 40 boats surrounding and chasing the dolphins. Tourists were instructed to jump into the water between moving boats in an attempt to get close to them. It felt dangerous for both the tourists and the dolphins. The animals were clearly being harassed and stressed. This should not be promoted as a tourist attraction.
After this disappointing experience, we finally went snorkeling. Unfortunately, the snorkeling spot was completely unsuitable. The current was extremely strong, making it difficult and exhausting to swim. There were also huge numbers of jellyfish, and we were stung repeatedly. To make matters worse, we could constantly smell fuel and engine exhaust from the many boat motors around us while snorkeling, which completely ruined the experience and raised concerns about the environmental impact on the marine life. Even worse, our guide disappeared and was nowhere to be seen while we were struggling in the water. It felt genuinely unsafe.
At that point, we were already upset and told the guide that we wanted to return to the hotel immediately. This seemed to cause panic among the guides, as they clearly did not expect tourists to complain or refuse to continue. We had a serious argument before they finally agreed to take us back.
Please be aware of what you are supporting when booking these tours. Chasing dolphins with dozens of boats is not wildlife tourism—it is animal harassment. The noise, fuel fumes, and constant disturbance are harmful to both the animals and the overall experience. If you care about animal welfare, responsible tourism, and safety, I would strongly recommend avoiding this activity.

content: Mnemba is a barefoot paradise off the coast of Zanzibar. It's a place where the energy shifts from the moment you arrive. It's the staff who make you feel at home, the understated luxury with meticulous attention to detail that doesn't feel intrusive, and the nature that envelops and transforms you. Peace permeates the air! This is my second time at Mnemba, and this time after the renovations. It was beautiful before, and now it's simply unparalleled. The food is organic, healthy, light yet plentiful, and delicious! Every day is a surprise and a feast! Sundowners are a ritual; it's a sanctuary for marine animals and birds, although there are also small antelopes on the island. You reach Mnemba by boat from Muyuni, Zanzibar. The days unfold amidst the sun, the beach, snorkeling, scuba diving, paddleboarding, bush dinners, moonlight beach dinners, sunset dhow trips, holistic treatments, yoga and relaxation, and facial and body treatments at the spa! Wendy is the best massage therapist in the world! Or simply enjoy the stunning turquoise blue of the sea and wait for the tides to go out so you can walk on the sandbanks and feel like you're in heaven.

content:
I feel the need to share this because it was one of the most upsetting travel experiences I’ve had.
The “Blue Safari” dolphin tour in Tanzania is sold as a magical chance to swim with dolphins in their natural habitat but the reality is very different.
Dozens of boats chase the same dolphins at the same time. Instead of a peaceful encounter, the animals are surrounded and stressed, constantly trying to escape. Many even appear injured.
This is not respectful wildlife interaction, it’s harassment. Humans with engines versus wild animals trying to survive.
No one should support this. If you truly care about animals, please think twice before booking it.

content:
Mbemba was the first stop on our wonderful stay in Zanzibar, and believe me, the most spectacular along with the Blue Lagoon Safari, which I'll tell you about later.
When we arrived on this wonderful little island, we were immediately captivated by the spectacular white strip of sand that cuts into the ocean for a few hundred meters.
Turquoise water, a coral reef with countless varieties of tropical fish, and, as if by magic, we saw a colony of dolphins happily dancing in the distance, undeterred by the thought of us seeing them.
Perhaps they're accustomed, but they're also docile and less afraid of human presence than other cetaceans.
We immediately set off on the boat to get up close and take some photos. The tour guides also invited us to dive in and swim with them, which initially left me perplexed, but we were reassured; the dolphins here are accustomed, so my children and I jumped in immediately with immense joy.
It was a pure spectacle, magnificent to be so close. and watch their pirouettes underwater.
We stayed in this stretch of water for a good half hour, then the dolphins disappeared.
We returned to the Mbemba sandbar, relaxed and sunbathed on the beach. Afterwards, the program included snorkeling in the coral reef, which is truly extraordinary for its rich coral and fish of every kind and color.
After snorkeling, the excursion concluded with lunch on the island, which was entirely seafood-based. We've never eaten so many lobsters and sea squirts as in Zanzibar, as I believe in many other tropical countries.
Everything was truly top-notch.

content:
I'm shocked by how many people in these reviews rave about the amazing experience of swimming with turtles.
I found it absolutely awful.
To be fair, we hadn't really done our research beforehand because we met two girls who spontaneously invited us along.
We paid the entrance fee ($15 for 30 minutes) and went in.
We immediately noticed the astonishing number of turtles gathered in one spot (something you don't usually see in the wild) and asked if the animals could actually swim in and out on their own.
We were told that was practically impossible, and that's when we finally realized that these weren't wild turtles, but rather captured turtles brought there to entertain tourists.
As soon as you start questioning the ethical aspects of the whole thing, you're immediately told that it's a "rescue center"—which is simply a blatant lie.
We were told that this was practically impossible. The animals clearly have no wounds or other externally visible problems; they can't be sick either, since sick animals in the wild are almost always infested with parasites.
Proper rescue centers therefore have various sterile pools where the animals' problems can truly be addressed.
Furthermore, rescue centers house WILD animals! This means that, for obvious reasons, it's not allowed for random tourists to enter the water with these animals. Besides, the animals would be sick or injured, which is why you shouldn't go in the water with them. (Generally, this is a good indicator of an ethical rescue center. In proper centers, visitors are not allowed to have direct contact with the animals.)
Then we were told that the animals are released again and again – after we asked several times and expressed our concerns, we were given a few more facts.
The turtles that end up in these "caves" are bycatch. (This includes animals that unfortunately get caught in large fishing nets, such as dolphins, sea urchins, squid, whales, and turtles.)
So, in the end, these are perfectly healthy animals that suffer because of our massive fish consumption.
They then serve as tourist attractions for a while until, under a grand guise of "animal welfare," they are released back into their natural habitat.
In short: after a few minutes of discussion, we left immediately and asked for a refund (15 dollars is easily a full day's budget for backpackers), which, of course, we didn't receive.
Please, in the name of animal welfare, do not support such facilities! In the wild, you can easily see turtles in their natural habitat on ethical boat tours without them having to suffer.

We had a fabulous visit to Salam Cave swimming with the turtles. There are so many of them and they’re incredibly friendly - although definitely watch out because they can bite. Speaking from experience… but honestly, the bite was worth it!
Top tip: don’t wear green swimwear unless you want the turtles mistaking you for the seaweed they’re being fed!

content:
One of the most unique experiences we had in Zanzibar.
When we first arrived, it was honestly difficult to imagine that such a beautiful cave was hidden there. The area was undergoing some improvements and construction work, so at first glance it does not immediately reveal what is waiting below.
Before entering the water, visitors are asked to shower thoroughly to remove sunscreen, body lotions and other products. We really appreciated this, as it shows how seriously they take the protection of the turtles and their environment.
Once inside, the experience is incredible. The water is crystal clear, the cave itself is beautiful, and we were even able to spot bats hanging from the ceiling. It feels like entering a hidden world.
The turtles are the main attraction and getting so close to them is something truly special. Visitors are given seaweed to feed them, and the turtles quickly swim over looking for a snack. Being able to observe them from such a short distance was unforgettable.
We paid for the one-hour experience, although for many visitors the 30-minute option would probably be enough. Either way, it was well worth it.
One funny piece of advice: avoid wearing green swimwear! My wife was wearing a green swimsuit, and one of the turtles apparently mistook it for seaweed and gave her a little bite on the back. Later, I had a small piece of seaweed attached to my arm and ended up getting a bite as well. Nothing serious at all, but it definitely gave us a good laugh and became one of the funniest memories of the experience.
The facilities are still being improved, and customer service could perhaps be a little more polished in some areas, but it was clear that the team is investing in the site and working to make the experience even better.
Overall, this was an immersive and memorable experience that allowed us to get closer to these amazing animals than we ever expected. The conservation aspect of the project was also very interesting, and learning that the turtles are cared for before eventually being released made the visit even more meaningful.
If you are visiting Zanzibar and enjoy nature and wildlife, Salaam Cave Aquarium is definitely worth adding to your itinerary.
Highly recommended.

content:
Visiting Salaam Cave to feed my favorite animals—the turtles—was truly a wonderful and unforgettable experience. From the moment you arrive, everything is well organized and focused on both safety and respect for the animals. Before entering the cave, you’re required to shower off, and a staff member walks you through a set of simple rules to follow. You’re also given a small container of seaweed to feed the turtles.
The water is cold at first, which can be a bit of a shock, but once you’re in, it becomes comfortable. One of the best tips is to stay calm and move gently. Feeding the turtles small pieces of seaweed helps make the experience last longer and keeps them engaged.
I truly believe the turtles can sense energy and tension. By remaining calm, gentle, and not anxious, the turtles were very peaceful with me. Some tourists who were in the water at the same time seemed scared and tense, and they ended up getting bitten. I, however, did not get bitten at all, even after I ran out of seaweed.
Overall, it was a beautiful, peaceful experience. If you respect the rules, stay calm and treat the turtles gently, visiting Salaam Cave is an incredible experience I would highly recommend—especially for anyone who loves marine life as much as I do. We did not go with a tour guy- went on our own which is a lot better option. $12 per person for 30minutes

content:
⭐ SOS ⭐ Disturbing Treatment of a poor Monkey Baby 🐒
I visited Saalam Cave in November witnessed something extremely upsetting. A young monkey was kept on a short chain next to a “donations” box, apparently for paid photos with tourists. The animal showed clear signs of severe stress — it jumped at visitors and even bit someone. Its only “toy” was an electrical cable, which is dangerously unsafe.
After speaking with animal welfare groups, I learned that situations like this often involve young monkeys being taken from the wild, sometimes violently.
Supporting such practices — even unintentionally — contributes to more animals being captured and mistreated.
⚠️Please try to convince the handler to give you the monkey freely — and importantly, do not make any payment.
If you are able to take the monkey into your care, please contact the animal welfare organizations in Zanzibar immediately.
If you need a contact, feel free to message me on Instagram: @atzimieze ⚠️
I strongly urge all visitors:
• Please do not pay for photos or donate money when animals are being exploited.
• If you witness this monkey or others in distress, speak up and report it.
• Please also report this location directly on Google Maps (“Report this place”) so authorities and platforms are alerted. The more reports they receive, the faster something can change.
• Share this information with other travelers — your voice matters.
This experience was heartbreaking, and I sincerely hope that this monkey receives help as soon as possible. Tourism should never come at the expense of animal welfare. Let’s make sure practices like this have no place here.

content:
I went to Salaam Cave very early right when they opened at 7:30 am. I think the opening time is flexible. The cost to get in is 12 USD for 30 minutes in the water, it’s more for an hour. I believe this to be a fair price compared to many other attractions around.
Guides are there to point out any information you may need. The pool is underground. Be advised for those with mobility issues, the staircase down into the cave is very steep. The water can be difficult to navigate with many rocks, pebbles, and sea turtles coming at you. It is best to navigate slowly and calmly.
From my experience, sea turtles do not bite you randomly. The only rare instances of biting happen when you are not careful feeding them so they bite your hand. With caution you should be more than fine.

content:
Absolutely not recommended – animal suffering for mass tourism
I am shocked by the way the turtles are treated here. It's pure mass tourism – far too many people are herded through at once, it's loud, chaotic, and completely disrespectful to the animals.
The turtles are kept in an artificial pool marketed as a "cave" – but there's no discernible exit or natural retreat for them. They are clearly being fed to get close to visitors. Some tourists touch the animals, even push them away or scream loudly. There's absolutely no consideration for the animals – and no real control by the staff.
From my perspective, the turtles seem completely stressed; some are even snapping at each other. This whole thing has absolutely nothing to do with respecting nature or animal welfare. For $12, you get 30 minutes in an overcrowded, noisy setting designed solely to rush tourists through.
For me, this was a disturbing experience. I can only advise everyone against it – please don't support such things.

content:
Salaam Cave Aquarium offers a unique opportunity to interact with turtles in a natural cave pool setting, but sadly, the overall experience falls short in many critical areas. The only standout feature was the excellent videography service provided by one of the staff members—though even this requires haggling to get a reasonable price.
Visitor management is lacking, with far too many people allowed into the pool at once, raising concerns about the turtles’ well-being. There’s no visible system to refresh or filter the water regularly, which is alarming considering the pollution caused by constant human activity. For an attraction that charges a premium fee, the showers and restrooms are subpar and in need of serious improvement.
There are also safety issues. The turkeys on site, likely stressed by captivity, can be aggressive and are prone to biting. Visitors should also tread carefully inside the cave—the uneven rock floor is quite slippery and could lead to injury if one isn’t cautious.
Most disappointing is the lack of education or orientation. A brief welcome speech explaining the cave’s significance and the conservation efforts for the turtles, including their eventual release, would go a long way in improving the experience.
Overall, an average and somewhat underwhelming visit.

content:
OMG, this place is amazing, I would give 10* if it was possible!!
It's a small cave where injured turtles are cared for and rehabilitated before being released back into the sea.
You pay a small fee at the gate for 1/2 hour or 1 hour and have a guide to explain the process. We brought some seaweed, and as we already had our swimmers on, we went down the ladder into the cave. They do have changing rooms you can use for free.
Once in the cave, we left our bags on the platform, I gave our guide my phone, and we went down another ladder into the water. The water is fresh at first and comes to waist height if you are 5ft 9, the floor of the cave was very rocky.
As soon as we were in the water, the turtles swam over to us, and we fed them some seaweed. Just watch your fingers as one turtle was quite greedy and nipped my thumb!
They don't mind you being there and swimming around you. They are very gentle, and you can pet them when they swim past. There are yellow birds that have made their nests above you in the cave.
We got out after half an hour, and our guide gave me my phone back with lots of amazing pictures and videos of me in the water with the turtles. It was a truly lovely time and not too busy when we visited, about 2pm.

- Entry to the cave should be limited to a certain number of people. We arrived 5 minutes before a group of 12 who were incredibly loud and inconsiderate. We were then asked to leave after 30 minutes, even though we wanted to leave ourselves anyway because it was getting too crowded.
- When it was less crowded, we were only allowed back in "as an exception" for a quick photo.

Those who are easily startled and move suddenly in the water should, out of consideration for the animals (which also lie on the bottom and are at risk of being stepped on), watch from the rocks and not go into the water. Furthermore, sunscreen should be avoided for the 30 minutes to prevent polluting the water and the cave.
All in all, a fantastic experience!

content: Chameleons are a family of lizards that can change their body color depending on the situation, primarily to protect themselves from danger, especially predators such as snakes and monkeys. They are adapted to an arboreal lifestyle, so here in the small garden, trees and small bushes have been created for them, along with burrows for burying eggs. The staff feeds them once a day, providing 5-7 insects each. The breeding center currently houses 18 adult chameleons. The chameleons live solitary lives, pairing up only during mating season. According to the guide, male chameleons may fight among themselves to assert dominance. These lizards are completely harmless to humans and very friendly. We got the impression that they perceive us as large trees, interesting to climb and explore. Chameleons use their paws and tail for balance and stability. When touching human skin, they do so very gently and tenderly. They catch insects offered for food with their tongues, which have a suction cup at the end. The process of ejecting the tongue lasts only 1/20th of a second—very quickly, as you can see in the video. Overall, we spent about half an hour here with a guide, and it was very interesting. The guide speaks excellent English and explains all the details of caring for the lizards, answering all questions very well. This is a place to visit for people of all ages. Considering the nearby caves, which I would recommend limiting to older people and children, a visit to the small chameleon nursery will fully justify your visit to Tazari village. The cost of visiting the nursery is only five dollars. The village is a 15-minute tuk-tuk ride from Nuvi. The road is mostly on the highway, but then you'll turn onto a secondary road. Tuk-tuk fares vary widely, but we settled on 20,000 shillings roundtrip and paid on the way back. This was the right decision, as the driver would likely have doubled the price if we'd paid 20,000 upfront.

content:
Avoid at all costs… I am so shocked by the lack of respect shown to animals on Earth for the sake of tourist entertainment.
Especially in Zanzibar. Between the various salam caves (turtle attractions) and dolphin fishing, you'll find these kinds of mini-zoos all over the island, like the one in Nungwi. The number of animals living on less than a hectare of land is appalling, and on top of that, the number of tourists disrupts their lives and natural rhythms.
Everything has become a business… for a quick photo with a chameleon on your hand, you can't imagine their tiny hearts and their tiny metabolisms, but they are very fragile, and what you are doing is cruel. It's a crime to make them suffer like this.
Please don't go! Even if they say they release them after getting them used to humans and feeding them, do you think they will be able to hunt insects and then adapt to their real environment? … I have so many questions.

From the moment we arrived, we were warmly welcomed by the sweetest guide and the kind-hearted owner, who made us feel like VIP guests throughout the entire visit. What made this tour so special was that it was completely private — just the two of us — which allowed for a relaxed, intimate, and truly personal experience.

From handmade spice necklaces to small samples of fresh local produce — it was beyond generous and heartwarming. We felt so appreciated and connected to the people behind this beautiful place.
This is not your average spice tour — it’s a heartwarming, authentic, and deeply personal experience that we will cherish forever. If you’re in Zanzibar, do yourself a favor and visit this farm. You won’t regret it for a second.
Thank you again for the unforgettable memories — we will carry them with us always! ❤️🌴

content: Abdillah was a fantastic guide. His motivation to learn languages ​​(English and French) and his knowledge of the local fauna were truly impressive! We booked directly with the farm. The tour (approximately 90 minutes) plus a fruit snack cost $5 per person. Afterwards, we bought some spices and left a tip. A wonderful experience!

clauses.clause_text: Afterwards, we bought some spices and left a tip.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: What a great adventure - do not miss this! Bilal our guide and owner was so nice and knowledgeable on all the plants and spices there. He really involved everybody on the tour in this experience and made it fun - would be great for kids too. Really a hands on experience for all. Bilai mentioned that his company does various languages including French, German and Italian. There is so much more here than just spices including some surprises at the end. Please take advantage of this opportunity. My pictures don’t do this place justice.

clauses.clause_text: My pictures don’t do this place justice.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
A very informative and interesting 3-hour tour with Mohammed! He explained everything wonderfully and livened things up with a few stories.
It wasn't at all like a sales pitch, and there was no pressure to buy anything. The spices are all very affordable, and there's a great selection.
The tour only costs 10 TZS / $5 per person, which is absolutely worth it 😊 At the end of the tour, you get a fruit tasting.
Highly recommended!!

clauses.clause_text: It wasn't at all like a sales pitch, and there was no pressure to buy anything.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: We visited this farm with our family of four. We paid 25 each plus tips for the guides and tree climber. There was some confusion about the tour when we booked through Zantours who had not been to this farm before (we picked it because it was close to our hotel). They should have communicated in advance as we thought we were paying through Zantours and the spice farm wanted direct payment. Setting that aside, while the guide was nice and it was fun to see how all the spices are grown, the cost of this tour is not reflective of the experience. I thought that there was a cooking class included in this price but that is an add on. I ended up canceling another tour with Zantours because I felt ripped off after this one. The locals in Zanzibar think all North Americans are rich (and relatively speaking I guess we are) and so have no problem charging high tour rates for everything. They don’t realize that some of us saved up for a year to take this once in a lifetime trip. Wouldn’t recommend this tour to others.

clauses.clause_text: They should have communicated in advance as we thought we were paying through Zantours and the spice farm wanted direct payment.
I ended up canceling another tour with Zantours because I felt ripped off after this one.
Wouldn’t recommend this tour to others.

The tasting of different spices during the tour was very enjoyable, as was the little break at the end with pineapple and watermelon.

It was a very good experience. The price was very reasonable.

clauses.clause_text: The tour lasted approximately two hours.

Otherwise, an excellent experience!

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni

content:
Nous avons fait une visite de près de 2 heures. Fatima notre guide était excellente et amusante, elle nous a appris et fait découvrir pleins de fruits, légumes racines et épices. C'est tellement surprenant que chaque plante, brindille ou feuille à une surprise à nous faire découvrir. La visite était vraiment enrichissante.
Malheureusement notre visite à été écourtée puisqu'un autre groupe nombreux est arrivé. Nous, nous étions que deux. De ce que j'ai compris, un autre guide ne s'est pas présenté. Notre guide Fatima a donc dû assister le nouveau groupe. Notre visite s'est donc terminé avant la fin :(
Le ' nouveau guide'" un monsieur très gentil mais il ne parlait que swahili. Ils nous ont quand même fait faire la dégustation de fruits et la démonstration de la montée du cocotier. Nous avons reçus nos couronnes et bijoux en feuilles et fleurs qu'ils ont fabriqués devant nous.
